muscles.name: Protractor pectoralis / cucullaris
muscles.developmental: Branchiomeric. Derives from cranial paraxial/lateral plate mesoderm caudal to the last pharyngeal arch, not from somites — the defining muscle of the head–trunk boundary.

consensus.origin: Fascia over the occiput and anterior epaxial/axial musculature; in gnathostome fishes, the dorsal edge of the branchial region.
consensus.insertion: Dorsal margin of the pectoral girdle — scapula, suprascapula, or cleithrum.
consensus.action: Protracts and stabilises the pectoral girdle against the head and axial skeleton; in mammals, elevates and rotates the scapula.
consensus.innervation: Accessory nerve (CN XI) or its non-mammalian equivalent — caudal branchial branches of the vagus complex. Not spinal.

occurrences.name: Cucullaris
occurrences.action: Elevates the branchial arches and stabilises the girdle.
occurrences.attachmentNote: Squalus acanthias. The information was in this row's own `origin`/`insertion` prose and had never been structured; Ziermann et al. also resolve the insertion further than the prose did, naming the scapular process, the posterior epibranchial cartilages and the anterior extrabranchial cartilages as three separate ends. No origin row: the sheet arises from the fascia beside the epaxial musculature and touches no element there, which is why a muscle that spans the head-trunk boundary leaves nothing for a fossil to record at its front end. The same dissection failed to find the 'levatores arcuum branchialium' of Kesteven (1942) in either Squalus or Mustelus laevis, so the levator half of this record's Chondrichthyes name is on Kesteven's authority and not on theirs.

occurrences.name: Protractor pectoralis
occurrences.note: Lepisosteus osseus. The cucullaris develops from the same cranial mesoderm population as the branchial constrictors, supporting a branchiomeric rather than somitic origin. Naumann et al. also report that the muscle has been misidentified in earlier work on this fish.

occurrences.name: Protractor pectoralis (cucullaris)
occurrences.action: Draws the girdle anterodorsally.
occurrences.innervation: Accessory nerve equivalent; developmentally distinct from the levator scapulae, which is somitic.
occurrences.note: Sefton et al. (2016) show the cucullaris and the somitic levator scapulae are separable by developmental origin even where they are topographically adjacent — the strongest available test of this homology.
occurrences.attachmentNote: Two heads arising together and diverging posteriorly. The anterior head lands between the procoracohumeralis and the dorsalis scapulae, which is the topological fix on its identity.
occurrences.origin: Dorsal fascia and the posterior surface of the skull.
occurrences.insertion: Anterior head onto the lateral surfaces of the procoracoid and scapula; posterior head onto the anterolateral border of the scapula.

occurrences.name: Protractor pectoralis
occurrences.attachmentNote: Timon lepidus. Origin: Occipital region and cervical fascia. Insertion: Anterior margin of the scapula and suprascapula. Not yet resolved to skeleton.json ids — this is the source's prose, carried here so it is not mistaken for a scored attachment.

occurrences.name: Protractor pectoralis (episternocleidomastoideus, partim)
occurrences.attachmentNote: Alligator and Crocodylus, from Meers's descriptions. Meers's m. trapezius, this record's crocodylian occurrence. A thin sheet from the thoracodorsal fascia ventrolateral to the median row of dorsal scutes, inserting fleshily in Crocodylus acutus and by an aponeurotic sheet in other species along the cranial edge of the scapula dorsal to the acromion. Its origin can look continuous with that of latissimus dorsi but is always separable. **No acromion row, and that is now a decision rather than a workaround.** The acromion is scored present in Crocodylia (see skeleton.json), but Meers places this insertion *dorsal to* it, on the cranial edge of the scapula — the acromion is his reference point, not the attachment site. Two other crocodylian muscles in this dataset do attach to it.

occurrences.name: Cucullaris capitis / cucullaris cervicis
occurrences.attachmentNote: Gallus domesticus. Insertion: Clavicle and scapula. Not yet resolved to skeleton.json ids — this is the source's prose, carried here so it is not mistaken for a scored attachment.

occurrences.name: Trapezius (+ sternocleidomastoideus)
occurrences.action: Elevates, retracts and rotates the scapula.
occurrences.innervation: Accessory nerve (CN XI), with a proprioceptive contribution from the cervical ventral rami.
occurrences.note: The mammalian trapezius and sternocleidomastoid are subdivisions of a single cucullaris field. Their retention of CN XI innervation, despite lying entirely within the neck and trunk, is the classic evidence that innervation tracks developmental origin rather than topographic position.
occurrences.attachmentNote: Galictis cuja. Trapezius, both bellies. Pars cervicalis from the cervical raphe between C3-4 and T1, pars thoracica from the thoracic raphe between T2 and T8, inserting on the distal two-thirds of the cranial margin of the scapular spine and often reaching the metacromion. Every origin is raphe or fascia, not bone — which is why a muscle this large leaves so little for a fossil to record.

homology.notes: Homology of the cucullaris across gnathostomes is supported by three independent lines: branchiomeric developmental origin, accessory/vagal innervation, and consistent topology between the occiput and the girdle. Sefton et al. (2016) resolved the long-standing question of whether the tetrapod cucullaris is head or trunk muscle in favour of head.
homology.teaching: The single best example of innervation as a homology criterion. A muscle that ends up in the shoulder still carries a cranial nerve.

muscles.name: Serratus anterior
muscles.developmental: Somitic (abaxial); derived from the ventrolateral lips of the cervical and anterior thoracic somites.

consensus.origin: Lateral surfaces of the anterior ribs and/or the transverse processes of the cervical vertebrae, by a series of digitations.
consensus.insertion: Medial (costal) surface of the scapula, typically along and near its vertebral border.
consensus.action: Suspends the trunk from the girdle in a sling; protracts, retracts and rotates the scapula depending on which digitations contract.
consensus.innervation: Long thoracic nerve (ventral rami of the anterior spinal nerves entering the brachial plexus; C5–C7 in mammals).

occurrences.name: Serratus anterior
occurrences.note: Part of the 'serrati' sensu Howell (1937a).
occurrences.attachmentNote: Ambystoma ordinarium. Origin: Anterior ribs and transverse processes. Insertion: Medial surface of the suprascapular cartilage and scapula. Not yet resolved to skeleton.json ids — this is the source's prose, carried here so it is not mistaken for a scored attachment.

occurrences.name: Serratus anterior
occurrences.note: Part of the 'serrati' sensu Howell (1935, 1937b).

occurrences.name: Serratus anterior
occurrences.note: Retained despite the carapace; the girdle sits inside the rib cage in turtles, so the sling geometry is unlike that of any other tetrapod.

occurrences.name: Serratus anterior
occurrences.note: = serratus ventralis sensu Kardong & Zalisko (1998), Kardong (2002).

occurrences.name: Serratus anterior
occurrences.note: = serratus ventralis sensu Meers (2003).
occurrences.attachmentNote: Crocodylus porosus. Originates from the ventrolateral ribs and inserts by tendon along the entire MEDIO-POSTERIOR scapular margin — a broad, thin girdle extensor. Two insertion rows because the source names two aspects of one bone; a single `lateral` row had been standing here, which is the aspect the global side table supplies and not the one the paper gives.

occurrences.name: Serratus superficialis + profundus
occurrences.attachmentNote: Gavia immer CM 2320, and the record covers BOTH muscles named in its title, which is why there is a cervical origin. SUPERFICIALIS: pars cranialis has only one head of origin in loons — fleshy on the lateral surface of the shaft of the first true rib — inserting by tendon on the ventral margin of the proximal quarter of the scapula between the heads of the subscapularis; pars caudalis arises by aponeurosis from the lateral surface of the 4th sternal rib and the 1st and 2nd true ribs. PROFUNDUS has three heads, and the cranial one is the reason for the vertebral row: it arises from the LAST CERVICAL VERTEBRAE, not from a rib, and inserts on the DORSOMEDIAL surface of the distal half of the scapula, while the middle and caudal heads arise by tendinous sheets from the lateral surface of the true ribs and insert on the central and distal thirds of the ventromedial scapular blade. Both of those had been missing while the rows carried only the superficialis' rib origin and a single ventral scapular row. Pars metapatagialis of the superficialis stays out deliberately: it inserts into the HUMERAL FEATHER TRACT, not onto bone, and is one of the avian muscles that cannot leave an osteological trace at its distal end.

occurrences.name: Serratus ventralis cervicis + thoracis
occurrences.origin: Cervicis as six slips from the cervical ribs of vertebrae II to VII; thoracis as four or five slips from the first four or five ribs, the foremost occupying the whole length of the first rib from tubercle to costal cartilage.
occurrences.insertion: Cervicis in fans on the internal surface of the scapula; thoracis on the caudal angle of the scapula, on the internal as well as the external side.
occurrences.attachmentNote: Tachyglossus aculeatus. This replaces a row giving the origin as 'ribs 1-8 and the cervical transverse processes'. Gambaryan et al. put the cervical slips on the cervical RIBS, one per vertebra from the axis back, and the thoracic slips on four or five ribs, not eight.

occurrences.name: Serratus anterior (serratus ventralis)
occurrences.action: Protracts and upwardly rotates the scapula; holds the medial border against the thorax.
occurrences.attachmentNote: Galictis cuja. Serratus ventralis cervicis from the dorsal tubercles of the transverse processes of C3-C7 and the first two or three ribs; serratus ventralis thoracis from the ribs of T2-T3 to T6-T7. All fascicles converge onto the medial surface of the dorsal edge and caudal angle of the scapula, sharing fibres with the rhomboidei.

occurrences.name: Serratus anterior
occurrences.attachmentNote: Eudyptes pachyrhynchus, Schreiweis's type species. Serratus profundus, four flat fleshy fascicles from the last two cervical and first two thoracic ribs dorsal to the uncinate processes, inserting on about the caudal half of the costal scapula near the vertebral border. The small cranial fascicle is usually absent in Spheniscus and Megadyptes. A wing-propelled diver: the flipper is the most derived forelimb in Aves, and these rows are an observation of a penguin, not of birds. That is exactly what species-level scoring is for — the old model refused this source rather than let it stand for the clade.

occurrences.name: Serratus ventralis cervicis + thoracis
occurrences.origin: Cervicis as six slips from the cervical ribs of vertebrae II to VII, one per vertebra, the atlas excepted; thoracis as four slips from the lower halves of the first four ribs, short of the costal cartilages.
occurrences.insertion: Cervicis on the internal surface of the scapula, each slip spreading as a flat fan and each successive fan set lower and wider than the last; thoracis fused into one before reaching the scapula and inserting on the external side of the caudal angle, just cranial to the scapular slip of the latissimus spinalis.
occurrences.attachmentNote: Zaglossus bruijnii. The serratus ventralis thoracis is underdeveloped against the cervicis, the reverse of the therian balance, because the dorsal border of the monotreme scapula lies in the cervical region rather than over the thorax — so the body's weight is transmitted through the cervical part of the sling.
occurrences.divisionNote: The slips from the last three cervical vertebrae bifurcate into a subvertical main portion and a subhorizontal accessory portion. Gambaryan et al. argue the accessorius is additional to the therian condition rather than a subdivision of it — therians have the proprius alone — and that the homonomic monotreme series is the most primitive among living tetrapods, more complete than the bifurcating caudal slips Miner (1925) found in urodeles and Sphenodon.

occurrences.name: Serratus ventralis cervicis + thoracis
occurrences.origin: Cervicis as six slips from the cervical ribs of vertebrae II to VII; thoracis as three slips from the lower halves of the first three ribs, short of the costal cartilages.
occurrences.insertion: Cervicis gathered near the dorsal and cranial borders of the internal surface of the scapula, occupying much less of that surface than in the echidnas because the subscapularis has taken most of it; thoracis compactly on the external side of the caudal angle, fusing near its insertion with the main portion of the last cervical slip.
occurrences.attachmentNote: Ornithorhynchus anatinus. Five of the six cervical slips bifurcate here against three in Tachyglossidae, which Gambaryan et al. count as the derived state, while the retreat of the cervicis from the internal face of the scapula is the counterpart of the subscapularis moving onto it.

homology.notes: Present in every limbed tetrapod examined; a stable row across all six columns of Abdala & Diogo's Table 1. Subdivision into cervical and thoracic parts is a mammalian elaboration, not a new muscle.

consensus.origin: Axial skeleton — occiput, nuchal ligament, or the neural spines of the anterior vertebrae.
consensus.insertion: Vertebral (dorsal) border of the scapula or suprascapula.
consensus.action: Retracts and elevates the scapula; holds the vertebral border against the trunk.
consensus.innervation: Dorsal scapular nerve in mammals (C4–C5).

occurrences.note: Howell (1937b) and Abdala & Diogo's own dissections find no rhomboid muscle in urodeles. Some authors' 'basiscapularis' in urodeles runs occiput-to-scapula and is innervated by ventral rami of spinal nerves 1–2, but Smith (1926) himself listed basiscapularis as a synonym of the levator scapulae, not of a rhomboideus.

occurrences.name: 'Rhomboideus'
occurrences.note: Confirmed by dissection in Rhinella and described by Escariz de Peverelli (1965) in Bufo arenarum.
Never described in turtles and not found in Abdala & Diogo's dissections. Loss would be unsurprising given the carapace rigidly links the axial skeleton to the girdle.
Never described in lepidosaurs and not found by dissection.

occurrences.name: 'Rhomboideus'
occurrences.note: Reported by Howell (1937b), Dilkes (2000), Meers (2003) and confirmed by dissection.

occurrences.name: 'Rhomboideus' (superficialis + profundus)
occurrences.note: Sullivan (1962, 1967) report both a rhomboideus superficialis and a rhomboideus profundus.

occurrences.name: 'Rhomboideus' (superficialis + profundus)
occurrences.attachmentNote: Gavia immer CM 2320. Superficialis arises by aponeurosis from the last cervical vertebrae and the dorsal vertebrae cranial to the ala preacetabularis ilii, inserting semitendinously on the head of the scapula, on the dorsomedial surface of the proximal three-quarters of the scapular blade, and cranially on the dorsomedial surface of the dorsal end of the clavicle. Profundus lies almost entirely deep to it, arises by a broad aponeurosis from the same vertebrae and inserts along the length of the blade. The clavicular insertion is the row worth noting: it is the one that disappears in taxa whose clavicles fuse into a furcula differently. In Gavia immer USNM 504983 the superficial muscle has two heads, the cranial one inserting partly onto the surface of the deltoideus major — a within-species difference between two specimens of the same species.

occurrences.name: Rhomboideus (capitis, cervicis, thoracis)
occurrences.attachmentNote: Galictis cuja. Four bellies — cervicis, thoracis, capitis and profundus. Cervicis, the largest, runs from the raphe between T1 and the atlas or axis onto the craniomedial dorsal edge of the scapula including the dorsal angle. Scored at the level the rows can carry; the four bellies are in `parts`.

occurrences.name: Rhomboideus
occurrences.origin: Transverse crest of the occiput and the dorsal midline of the whole neck; aponeurotic as far back as the neural spine of the epistropheus, then fleshy to the midline, meeting its opposite number above the nuchal ligament.
occurrences.insertion: Cranial portion on the uppermost part of the cranial border of the scapula, its cranial angle, and both faces of its dorsal border; caudal portion on the internal side of the caudal angle.
occurrences.attachmentNote: Zaglossus bruijnii.
occurrences.divisionNote: Incipiently divided in Tachyglossidae: the two portions run at sharply different fibre angles — the cranial anteroposteriorly, the caudal mediolaterally — and correspond to the therian rhomboideus capitis and thoracis without being separate muscles.

occurrences.name: Rhomboideus
occurrences.origin: Transverse crest of the occiput and the dorsal midline of the neck, aponeurotic to the neural spine of the epistropheus and fleshy behind it.
occurrences.insertion: Cranial portion on the uppermost cranial border of the scapula, its cranial angle and both faces of the dorsal border; caudal portion on the internal side of the caudal angle.
occurrences.attachmentNote: Tachyglossus aculeatus.

occurrences.name: Rhomboideus
occurrences.origin: Transverse crest of the occiput and the dorsal midline of the neck, the occipital part set further back from the origin of the clavoacromiotrapezius than in the echidnas.
occurrences.insertion: Internal side of the caudal part of the dorsal border of the scapula, as far as its caudal angle.
occurrences.attachmentNote: Ornithorhynchus anatinus. Undivided, against the two portions of both echidnas, and the insertion is correspondingly confined to the caudal half of the dorsal border.
occurrences.divisionNote: Single here against `heads` in Tachyglossidae, which puts the differentiation of the rhomboideus inside Monotremata rather than on its stem.

homology.notes: The name is quoted deliberately. Abdala & Diogo argue that on their phylogeny it is more parsimonious to treat the 'rhomboideus' as independently acquired in anurans, archosaurs and mammals (three steps) than as ancestral to Tetrapoda and lost in urodeles, turtles and lepidosaurs (four steps). The parsimony margin is one step, so the result is fragile — and it requires three independent origins of a muscle with the same origin, insertion, orientation and function. They flag the missing evidence explicitly: detailed dorsal pectoral muscle studies in more lepidosaurs and urodeles.
homology.openQuestion: Is the archosaur 'rhomboideus' homologous to the anuran and mammalian rhomboideus, or a convergent axio-scapular muscle? Innervation and development data for the anuran and crocodylian muscles would settle it.
homology.teaching: A worked example of parsimony being decisive by a single step, and of why authors quote a muscle name.

muscles.name: Levator scapulae
muscles.developmental: Somitic. In Ambystoma it derives mainly from somite 3 (Piekarski & Olsson 2007); Piatt (1938) implicated somites 2–4 together with the hypobranchial muscles.

consensus.origin: Cranium (often the cartilaginous operculum in urodeles) or the transverse process of the atlas and anterior cervical vertebrae.
consensus.insertion: Anterodorsal margin of the scapula/suprascapula.
consensus.action: Elevates and protracts the scapula.
consensus.innervation: Ventral rami of the first and second spinal nerves; in Ambystoma also by the hypoglossal nerve.

occurrences.name: Levator scapulae
occurrences.action: Elevates the girdle; the opercular portion is part of the aquatic sound-reception pathway.
occurrences.innervation: First spinal nerve and hypoglossal nerve.
occurrences.note: Voluminous in urodeles and includes the columellaris and opercularis of Duellman & Trueb (1986) and Carroll (2007). Piekarski & Olsson (2007) showed its development and innervation differ from those of the protractor pectoralis, refuting the older claim that the urodele levator scapulae derives from the cucullaris.
occurrences.attachmentNote: Ambystoma ordinarium. Origin: Cranium, often the cartilaginous operculum. Insertion: Suprascapula. Not yet resolved to skeleton.json ids — this is the source's prose, carried here so it is not mistaken for a scored attachment.

occurrences.name: Levator scapulae superioris
occurrences.note: In anurans such as Rana the ancestral urodele muscle is fully differentiated into two separate muscles: the levator scapulae superioris and the opercularis. The name 'opercularis' should therefore be restricted to anurans.

occurrences.name: Levator scapulae
occurrences.attachmentNote: Timon lepidus. Origin: Mainly the transverse process of the atlas. Insertion: Scapula. Not yet resolved to skeleton.json ids — this is the source's prose, carried here so it is not mistaken for a scored attachment.

occurrences.name: Levator scapulae
occurrences.attachmentNote: Crocodylus porosus. Origin with the neck muscles on the lateral cervical ribs; fleshy insertion running the ANTERIOR scapular border from its anterodistal tip to the glenohumeral joint. Largely obscured by the trapezius — which these authors could not model, because skinning removed it.

occurrences.name: Levator scapulae (dorsalis, intermedius, ventralis)
occurrences.origin: Dorsalis by a tendon from the ventral side of the occiput behind the detrahens mandibulae, converging with the common tendon of the other two portions from the ventral tubercle of the atlas wing; intermedius additionally by an accessory tendon and ventralis fleshy along the whole length of the epistropheal rib.
occurrences.insertion: Dorsalis on the internal side of almost the entire dorsal border of the scapula and the dorsal fifth of its cranial border; intermedius on the medial side of the next two-fifths of the cranial border; ventralis on the internal side of the remaining ventral two-fifths and the acromion.
occurrences.attachmentNote: Tachyglossus aculeatus. Unlike the long-beaked echidna and the platypus, no portion reaches the clavicle, and the intermedius insertion stays on the medial side of the cranial border instead of wrapping onto the external side.

occurrences.name: Levator scapulae (+ omotransversarius)
occurrences.innervation: Cervical ventral rami and the dorsal scapular nerve.
occurrences.attachmentNote: Galictis cuja. Omotransversarius, from the caudomedial aspect of the ventral surface of the atlas onto the caudal region of the metacromion and onto the deltoideus pars scapularis. Scored on the acromion: the metacromion is a carnivoran process of it and has no element of its own here.

occurrences.name: Levator scapulae (dorsalis, intermedius, ventralis)
occurrences.origin: Dorsalis by a wide aponeurosis from the ventral side of the occiput behind the detrahens mandibulae; intermedius from the capsule of the atlanto-occipital joint back onto the ventral border of the epistropheal rib; ventralis from the ventral border of the epistropheal rib.
occurrences.insertion: Dorsalis on the internal side of the dorsal border of the scapula; intermedius on the remaining cranial part of that border and the dorsal half of the cranial border; ventralis on the rest of the cranial border, the acromial process and the distal sixth of the clavicle.
occurrences.attachmentNote: Zaglossus bruijnii. The occipital origin is the widest of the three genera, and Gambaryan et al. use that spread to argue that the tight association with the atlas seen in therians and in the platypus is an advanced condition reached independently in each.

parts.name: Levator scapulae intermedius
parts.note: Gambaryan et al. find no therian counterpart and read it as lost in that lineage.

parts.name: Levator scapulae ventralis
parts.note: = m. atlantoacromialis of therians, and the m. levator claviculae of Diogo & Abdala (2010).

occurrences.divisionNote: Three portions, not the two this row previously carried. The intermedius is the interesting one: it has no therian counterpart, so the monotreme condition is not an unsplit version of the mammalian muscle but a more subdivided one.

occurrences.name: Levator scapulae (dorsalis, intermedius, ventralis)
occurrences.origin: All three portions mainly from the ventral tubercle of the atlas wing — dorsalis by a short flat tendon, intermedius by a longer one plus a thin accessory tendon from the atlanto-occipital joint capsule, ventralis by an aponeurosis separated from the other two by the scalenus, its posterior fibres running fleshy along the caudoventral border of the atlas wing to the epistropheal rib.
occurrences.insertion: Dorsalis on the internal side of the cranial three-fifths of the dorsal border of the scapula and the dorsal half of its cranial border; intermedius on a short segment of the cranial border below it; ventralis on the remaining ventral part of the cranial border, the acromial process and the distal fifth of the clavicle. All three cover both faces of the cranial border.
occurrences.attachmentNote: Ornithorhynchus anatinus. The origin has withdrawn almost entirely onto the atlas, which is the therian arrangement — and Gambaryan et al. argue it was reached independently here rather than shared, because the echidnas keep the wide occipital origin.

homology.notes: Distinguished from the protractor pectoralis/cucullaris by somitic rather than branchiomeric origin and by spinal rather than accessory innervation, despite adjacent topology. The urodele 'opercularis' is part of this muscle, not a separate one.
homology.teaching: Pair with the cucullaris. Two adjacent occiput-to-scapula muscles with different germ layers of origin and different nerves — topology alone cannot separate them, development and innervation can.

muscles.name: Opercularis
muscles.developmental: Somitic; a differentiated portion of the ancestral levator scapulae field.

consensus.origin: Suprascapular cartilage.
consensus.insertion: Operculum of the otic capsule (the cartilaginous plate in the fenestra ovalis).
consensus.action: Transmits substrate-borne vibration from the forelimb and girdle to the inner ear; also braces the girdle.
consensus.innervation: Ventral rami of the anterior spinal nerves.

occurrences.name: Opercularis
occurrences.note: Only in anurans is this a discrete muscle. Together with the levator scapulae superioris it accounts for the single urodele levator scapulae.
occurrences.attachmentNote: A pectoral girdle muscle inserting on the ear. Anuran-only, and only in anurans is it a discrete muscle.

occurrences.note: The structure called 'opercularis' in urodeles is topologically part of the levator scapulae, not an independent muscle (Hetherington & Tugaoen 1990). Walthall & Ashley-Ross (2006) disagree in practice, describing a discrete strap-like m. opercularis in Taricha running from the cartilaginous operculum of the otic capsule to the anterior edge of the suprascapula — and assigning it the opposite origin and insertion to the anuran record here. Presence is left at 'no' because a single dissection does not settle the homology argument, but the disagreement is the point: the same structure is a muscle or a part of one depending on which criterion is applied.

homology.notes: An anuran autapomorphy arising by subdivision of the levator scapulae. Functionally striking: it is a limb-girdle muscle that inserts on the ear.
homology.teaching: Terminology trap. 'Opercularis' in an amphibian paper means different things depending on whether the animal is a frog or a salamander.

consensus.origin: Sternum.
consensus.insertion: Coracoid.
consensus.action: Draws the coracoid toward the sternum, stabilising the girdle's ventral articulation.
consensus.innervation: Ventral rami of the anterior brachial plexus; nerve to subclavius (C5–C6) in mammals.

occurrences.note: Howell (1937b) confirms it is not a distinct muscle in urodeles or anurans.

occurrences.name: Sternocoracoideus
occurrences.note: Often divided into superficial and deep heads in Iguana and Sphenodon (Holmes 1977; Dilkes 2000).
Fürbringer (1876), Walker (1973), Holmes (1977) and Dilkes (2000) hold that it is not present as an independent muscle in crocodylians or turtles.

occurrences.name: Sternocoracoideus
occurrences.note: Present according to Dilkes (2000).
occurrences.attachmentNote: The only muscle on the internal surface of the thoracic cavity. From the dorsal surface of the craniolateral sternum (processus craniolateralis) and the first rib, to a large depression on the dorsal surface of the coracoid base. Matsuoka & Hasegawa suggest it keeps the coracoid-sternum connection flexible.

occurrences.name: Sternocoracoideus
occurrences.origin: Fleshy from the dorsal side of the sternal manubrium along the rim of the sternocoracoid joint and from the internal side of the ventral part of a calcified region of the first costal cartilage.
occurrences.insertion: Dorsal (internal) side of the medial border of the procoracoid.
occurrences.attachmentNote: Tachyglossus aculeatus. This corrects an insertion previously scored on the coracoid. Gambaryan et al. put it on the procoracoid in all three genera, and the distinction matters here because the costocoracoideus, which inserts alongside it, is the one that takes the coracoid.

occurrences.name: Subclavius
occurrences.action: Depresses and stabilises the clavicle.
occurrences.note: Rattus norvegicus, the mammal in Abdala & Diogo's Table 2. Howell (1937b) argued the placental subclavius corresponds to the sternocoracoideus of other tetrapods, the coracoid having been lost and its attachment transferred to the clavicle.
occurrences.attachmentNote: As the subclavius. With the coracoid gone the insertion transfers to the clavicle — Howell's (1937b) basis for the homology.

occurrences.name: Sternocoracoideus
occurrences.origin: By a short aponeurosis from the dorsal side of the sternal manubrium along the rim of the sternocoracoid joint and from the internal side of the sternal end of the first costal cartilage, adjoining the costocoracoideus from below.
occurrences.insertion: Dorsal (internal) side of the medial border of the procoracoid.
occurrences.attachmentNote: Zaglossus bruijnii. The insertion is on the PROCORACOID, not the coracoid, in all three genera. Sternocoracoid mobility is much reduced in monotremes, but Gambaryan et al. argue the muscle's long fibres show it is still real, and point to the overlapping left and right procoracoids as a remnant of the pronounced craniocaudal sternocoracoid sliding seen in urodeles and lizards.

occurrences.name: Sternocoracoideus
occurrences.origin: Fleshy from the dorsal side of the sternal manubrium along the rim of the sternocoracoid joint, from that joint's articular capsule, and from the internal side of the ventral segment of the first costal cartilage.
occurrences.insertion: Unipennate; the terminal aponeurosis inserts on the dorsal side of the medial border of the procoracoid in its posterior half, clear of the suture with the coracoid, while the most anterior fibres insert fleshy on the cartilaginous lining of the procoracoid border.
occurrences.attachmentNote: Ornithorhynchus anatinus. The only genus in which part of the insertion is onto cartilage rather than bone, and the only one whose origin takes in the joint capsule.

homology.notes: The sternocoracoideus–subclavius correspondence follows Howell (1937b) and is reviewed in detail by Diogo et al. (2009a). Mivart (1869) instead suggested the subclavius was part of the amphibian procoracohumeralis; Romer (1924) rejected this, deriving teres minor and deltoideus clavicularis from procoracohumeralis instead. The distribution is patchy enough (present in lepidosaurs, birds, monotremes; absent or disputed in turtles, crocodylians, amphibians) that independent acquisition cannot be excluded.

consensus.origin: Anterior ribs.
consensus.insertion: Coracoid.
consensus.action: Draws the coracoid toward the ribs; girdle stabilisation.
consensus.innervation: Ventral rami of the anterior brachial plexus.

occurrences.note: Walker (1973): not present as a distinct muscle in turtles.

occurrences.name: Costocoracoideus
occurrences.note: Frequently divided into pars superficialis and pars profunda.

occurrences.name: Costocoracoideus
occurrences.note: Usually divided into pars superficialis and pars profunda (Meers 2003).
occurrences.attachmentNote: Crocodylus porosus. Klinkhamer et al. separate a costocoracoideus PROFUNDUS, fleshy from the lateral margin of the first few ribs to the ventro-posterior margin of the coracoid — the two coracoid rows are its one attachment named on two aspects. The SUPERFICIALIS is not scored here and is the reason to keep this record open: it arises on the ventro-lateral first few ribs and inserts on the MEDIAL HUMERAL HEAD, so one of the two parts of this muscle bypasses the girdle and reaches the arm.

occurrences.note: Dilkes (2000): not present as an independent muscle in birds.

occurrences.name: Costocoracoideus
occurrences.origin: Fleshy from the cranial border of both the cartilaginous and the bony segments of the first rib.
occurrences.insertion: By a short aponeurosis on the dorsal side of the medial border of the coracoid, adjoining the sternocoracoideus at the procoracoid-coracoid suture.
occurrences.attachmentNote: Tachyglossus aculeatus. Together with the sternocoracoideus, the subcoracoideus and the supracoracoideus this is one of the four coracoid-plate muscles monotremes retain and therians have lost with the bone.

occurrences.name: Costoscapularis
occurrences.note: Rattus norvegicus, from Abdala & Diogo's Table 2. Howell (1937b) reports a 'costoscapularis' in placentals, the coracoid attachment having shifted to the scapula.

occurrences.name: Costocoracoideus
occurrences.origin: By a wide aponeurosis from the internal side of the first costal cartilage and the cranial border of the first rib itself.
occurrences.insertion: By a short aponeurosis on the dorsal (internal) side of the medial border of the coracoid, and also on the procoracoid just lateral to the posterior part of the sternocoracoideus.
occurrences.attachmentNote: Zaglossus bruijnii. The only genus whose costocoracoideus reaches the procoracoid as well as the coracoid.

occurrences.name: Costocoracoideus
occurrences.origin: Fleshy from the cranial border of the upper part of the first costal cartilage and the lower part of the first rib, rising slightly above the origin of the anterior slip of the serratus ventralis thoracis, with the scalenus wedged between them.
occurrences.insertion: Restricted to the posterior half of the dorsal side of the medial border of the coracoid, not reaching forward to the procoracoid suture.
occurrences.attachmentNote: Ornithorhynchus anatinus. The most restricted of the three insertions — it stops short of the suture that the short-beaked echidna's reaches and the long-beaked echidna's crosses.

homology.notes: Restricted to lepidosaurs, crocodylians and monotremes among the taxa surveyed. The homologies of the reptilian costocoracoideus and sternocoracoideus with the mammalian subclavius are reviewed by Diogo et al. (2009a).

muscles.name: Pectoralis
muscles.developmental: Somitic; ventral (flexor) muscle mass of the limb bud.

consensus.origin: Sternum, clavicle, interclavicle and adjacent ventral structures — a broad fan across the ventral midline.
consensus.insertion: Deltopectoral crest of the humerus.
consensus.action: Adducts and retracts the humerus; the principal propulsive muscle of the forelimb in sprawling gaits and the main downstroke muscle in flight.
consensus.innervation: Pectoral nerves — ventral (flexor) division of the brachial plexus.

occurrences.name: Ventral fin muscle mass (undivided)
occurrences.note: Chondrichthyans have an undivided ventral (adductor/depressor) fin mass; no discrete pectoralis is differentiated.

occurrences.name: Pectoralis
occurrences.note: One of the four muscles Molnar et al. reconstruct in tetrapodomorph fish with their highest confidence — deltoideus, pectoralis, the forearm flexors and the forearm extensors — because a correlate is identified in the fossil and the muscle is bracketed by lungfish, coelacanths and tetrapods.
occurrences.attachmentNote: Eusthenopteron foordi. Andrews & Westoll (1970a) read the ventral cleithral ridge as the anterior extent of the pectoralis origin and the proximal, preaxial extreme of the ventral humeral ridge as its insertion. Molnar et al. accept the ridge but not the process: Callier et al. (2009), comparing Ichthyostega humeri across growth stages, place the pectoralis process in the MIDDLE of the ventral ridge, which makes the preaxial 'pectoralis processes' reported in Rhizodus, Strepsodus, Sauripterus and Sterropterygion part of a continuous ridge. The insertion is therefore scored on the undivided ridge — not on a process, and not on the deltopectoral crest, which is where an earlier note here put it.

occurrences.name: Pectoralis
occurrences.note: Tiktaalik roseae. Molnar et al. interpret it as lacking a pectoralis process: the ventral humeral ridge is confluent with the entepicondyle and undivided, and they place the separation of the pectoralis from the coracobrachialis one node crownward, at the last common ancestor of Tetrapoda, marked by a distinct pectoralis process and coracobrachialis fossa. So the pectoralis is not resolvable as a separate muscle here, and the row records that rather than a presence. The paired sulci on the internal and external margins of its coracoid foramen do mark a musculotendinous bundle running from the dorsomedial coracoid to the ventral humerus (Shubin et al. 2006), but no source names the muscle.

occurrences.name: Pectoralis
occurrences.attachmentNote: Acanthostega gunnari. The deltopectoral crest occupies the anterior portion of the ventral humerus (Coates 1996), the pectoral and deltoid processes united into one crest. Ichthyostega and the Catskill humerus differ: there the pectoralis process is separated from the deltoid process by the prepectoral space and is confluent with the ventral humeral ridge instead, which Callier et al. (2009) and Ahlberg (2011) read as the pectoralis still emerging from a larger ventral muscle mass. No origin is scored — few stem-tetrapod fossils preserve the ventral edge of the coracoid plate, so Molnar et al. could not trace the ventral girdle origins.

occurrences.name: Pectoralis
occurrences.attachmentNote: Ossinodus pueri. A rugose, slightly recessed region on the posterior lateral wings of the interclavicle, read by Bishop (2014) as part of the pectoralis origin; one of the six muscles Molnar et al. reconstruct here with their highest confidence. They accept interclavicular scars for the superficial ventral muscles only tentatively, since the ventral coracoid plate that would carry the rest of the origin is rarely preserved. Striations distinct from the dermal ornamentation are reported on the interclavicle of Greererpeton too. No humeral insertion is itemised for this taxon.

occurrences.name: Pectoralis
occurrences.attachmentNote: The insertion resolves to the crista ventralis — the salamander name for the deltopectoral crest — rather than to the proximal humerus generally. A refinement in resolution, not a shift.
occurrences.origin: Midline aponeurosis, sternum, and the tendinous inscriptions of the rectus abdominis.
occurrences.insertion: Crista ventralis of the humerus.

occurrences.name: Pectoralis
occurrences.action: In anurans the pectoralis is a principal landing-force absorber rather than a propulsive muscle; its enlargement is part of the saltatory forelimb complex.

occurrences.name: Pectoralis
occurrences.attachmentNote: Leiopelma hochstetteri. The deltopectoral crest — crista ventralis — carries the insertion of both the deltoideus and the pectoralis, and in most anurans it runs further distally than in salamanders or any other tetrapod. Leiopelma's is relatively SHORT, tapering to disappear near the midpoint of the shaft, the plesiomorphic anuran condition also found in extinct subfossil species of the genus; strong jumpers such as Lithobates extend it much further. The paper's headline reading is that the deltoid grew in importance relative to the pectoralis, and that the crest's orientation follows from loading during LANDING rather than take-off.

occurrences.name: Pectoralis
occurrences.attachmentNote: Xenopus laevis. A prominent boss for the pectoralis insertion close to the POSTERIOR edge of the deltopectoral crest — a discrete correlate where most anurans have the muscle inserting along the crest generally. The pipid humerus is the most atypical in the order: the crest is short, almost straight in cross section and directed ventrally, with a biconcave proximal area. A second anuran species on this record, and it disagrees with the first.

occurrences.name: Pectoralis
occurrences.note: = pectoralis major sensu Wyneken (2001).
occurrences.attachmentNote: Trachemys scripta, from Walker (1973). A very large triangular muscle from much of the anterior plastron: the periphery of its attachment sweeps an arc from the midventral line just behind the plastral attachment of the acromion, back and laterally to the posterior boundary of the bridge of the shell. All fibres converge on a narrow tendon onto the flexor border of the lateral process of the humerus. Retractor and adductor, and Walker reads it as also rotating the girdle posteriorly during limb retraction.

occurrences.name: Pectoralis
occurrences.innervation: Pectoral branches arising from the ventral divisions of the brachial plexus; in South American lizards the plexus is typically formed from spinal nerves 5–9 with considerable interspecific variation in root composition (Navarro et al. 2023).
occurrences.note: Present in all major extant reptilian clades (Fürbringer 1876; Walker 1973; Holmes 1977; Dilkes 2000).

occurrences.name: Pectoralis
occurrences.note: Attachments are deliberately not scored for Alligator mississippiensis. Allen et al. measure this muscle's architecture and give no attachment sites; Abdala & Diogo's crocodylian exemplar is Caiman latirostris, not Alligator. The attachment rows this occurrence used to carry were Klinkhamer et al.'s description of Crocodylus porosus and have moved to their own occurrence.

occurrences.name: Pectoralis
occurrences.attachmentNote: Crocodylus porosus. Fleshy along the ventral midline from the interclavicle and the STERNAL RIBS; tendinous onto the proximo-ventral humerus at the deltopectoral crest. A very large sheet covering the whole superficial ventral chest. No sternal origin is scored: Klinkhamer et al. name the interclavicle and the sternal ribs, and sternal ribs are ribs — the earlier sternum row was not theirs.

occurrences.name: Pectoralis
occurrences.action: Wing downstroke. The largest muscle in the body of most flying birds.
occurrences.note: Includes the pectoralis pars thoracica sensu Maxwell & Larsson (2007). The penguin pectoralis thoracica arises from the lateral sternal edge posterior to the coracobrachialis caudalis and from the trabecula lateralis, with a ribbon-like pars subcutanea abdominalis. Schreiweis (1982) records that the SUPRACORACOIDEUS is very well developed relative to the pectoralis in penguins — the reverse of the flying-bird proportion, and consistent with a wing that generates thrust on both strokes underwater rather than only on the downstroke.
occurrences.attachmentNote: Gallus domesticus, Abdala & Diogo's avian exemplar. From the sternal keel, the furcula and the ribs onto the deltopectoral crest — the crista pectoralis in avian nomenclature.

occurrences.name: Pectoralis
occurrences.attachmentNote: Cygnus cygnus. The origin is in three overlapping layers — shallow clavicle, deep clavicle plus carina, and sternal plane plus rib cage — all fusing distally onto the crista pectoralis, the avian name for the deltopectoral crest. The rib attachment is INDIRECT, onto the surface of underlying muscle, which is why the rib row is the weakest of the three. Both pectoralis muscles together are about 11% of body mass.

occurrences.name: Pectoralis
occurrences.origin: Anterior quarter of the stem of the interclavicle, sparing its most cranial part, and further back from the sternum excluding the xiphoid process.
occurrences.insertion: A compact area on the ventral side of the pectoral crest of the humerus.
occurrences.divisionNote: Undivided, as in the other two genera. This replaces a `divided` row carrying a pectoralis superficialis and profundus, which is the therian condition Gambaryan et al. explicitly contrast monotremes with.
occurrences.attachmentNote: Tachyglossus aculeatus. The only one of the three with a sternal origin. The clavicle is NOT part of it — a clavicular origin previously scored here belongs to the clavodeltoideus.

occurrences.name: Pectoralis major / pectoralis profundus
occurrences.action: Adducts and medially rotates the humerus.

occurrences.name: Pectoralis
occurrences.origin: Anterior fifth of the stem of the interclavicle, sparing its most cranial part.
occurrences.insertion: Ventral side of the pectoral crest of the humerus, over about a tenth of the bone's length.
occurrences.divisionNote: Undivided. Gambaryan et al. find no separation into pectoralis superficialis and profundus in any monotreme and count the single sheet among the primitive features monotremes retain against therians.
occurrences.attachmentNote: Zaglossus bruijnii. The most restricted pectoralis of the three genera: interclavicle only, with no sternal or costal component, and the shortest humeral insertion.

occurrences.name: Pectoralis
occurrences.origin: Anterior fifth of the stem of the interclavicle, sparing its most cranial part, and the ventral (sternal) parts of the costal cartilages of the first five ribs.
occurrences.insertion: The whole length of the pectoral crest of the humerus, on its ventral side.
occurrences.attachmentNote: Ornithorhynchus anatinus. Costal rather than sternal behind the interclavicle, and the insertion runs the full length of the crest instead of occupying part of it — the widest pectoralis of the three, on the animal with the widest humerus.

homology.notes: Present in every limbed tetrapod. One of the least ambiguous rows in the comparative tables — origin, insertion, innervation and ventral-mass derivation are all congruent.
homology.teaching: Use as the anchor when introducing the ventral/flexor mass. Everything else in the ventral mass can be located relative to it.

muscles.name: Supracoracoideus
muscles.developmental: Somitic; ventral mass, but see homology note on the mammalian supraspinatus/infraspinatus.
synonyms: 'infraspinatus' (Diogo & Abdala 2010, for the monotreme muscle Gambaryan et al. 2015 call supracoracoideus)

consensus.origin: Lateral (external) surface of the coracoid and scapula, anterior/dorsal to the pectoralis origin.
consensus.insertion: Proximal humerus, on or near the deltopectoral crest and greater tubercle.
consensus.action: Protracts and abducts the humerus. In birds, uniquely, it is the upstroke muscle.
consensus.innervation: Supracoracoid nerve; suprascapular nerve (C5–C6) in mammals.

occurrences.name: Supracoracoideus
occurrences.note: Reconstructed from the homology hypotheses of Diogo et al. (2016) as much as from the correlate: Molnar et al. list it with the procoracohumeralis as reconstructable because similar muscles are present in extant lungfish, coelacanths and tetrapods.
occurrences.attachmentNote: Eusthenopteron foordi. An ill-defined ridge between the proximal extent of the ventral humeral ridge and the deltoid-supinator ridge, read by Andrews & Westoll (1970a) as the supracoracoideus insertion. It is one of two correlates identified in this taxon and in no other tetrapodomorph fish, which Molnar et al. flag as reason for caution. No landmark is asserted: the ridge is not one of the named correlates they carry through the character mapping.

occurrences.name: Supracoracoideus
occurrences.attachmentNote: Acanthostega gunnari. The proximal ventral surface of the humerus divides into a smooth anterior region and a rough, concave posterior one, read as the insertions of the supracoracoideus and the coracobrachialis respectively (Coates 1996); the same configuration is described in Baphetes, Crassigyrinus, Ichthyostega, Greererpeton and Tulerpeton. Both muscles are scored as humerus/ventral, because the anterior-posterior distinction between them lies within that surface rather than being a second side, and which region each muscle took is kept here where it reads as the argument it is.

occurrences.name: Supracoracoideus
occurrences.note: Ossinodus pueri. One of the six muscles Molnar et al. reconstruct here with their highest confidence, on the strength of correlates Bishop (2014) identified; they do not itemise which scar carries it, so no attachment row is scored.

occurrences.name: Supracoracoideus
occurrences.attachmentNote: Fan-shaped and parallel-fibred, its posterior part lying deep to the pectoralis and inserting beside it on the same crest. In salamanders the supracoracoideus is still a ventral adductor; the dorsal, wing-elevating role it takes in birds requires the triosseal canal, which does not exist here.
occurrences.origin: Ventral superficial surface of the coracoid cartilage.
occurrences.insertion: Crista ventralis of the humerus, adjacent to the pectoralis insertion.

occurrences.name: Supracoracoideus
occurrences.attachmentNote: Crocodylus porosus. Fleshy origin on the PROXIMO-LATERAL coracoid, covering the entire humeral head; fleshy insertion on the VENTRO-LATERAL humerus at the deltopectoral crest. Broad and triangular, forming much of the shoulder. Both aspects are stated by Klinkhamer et al. and both had been overwritten by the global side table, which gave coracoid/ventral and deltopectoral-crest/anterior — the one thing this source is cited for is that it names the aspect.

occurrences.name: Supracoracoideus complex (longus, intermedius, brevis)
occurrences.action: The primary protractors of the humerus; the brevis also adducts.
occurrences.innervation: Nerve to supracoracoideus, a branch of SN VIII, shared by all divisions.

parts.name: Supracoracoideus longus
parts.note: Fan-shaped and dominant. Extensive fleshy origin from the cranial half of the MEDIAL surface of the scapula and the adjacent coracoid opposite the glenoid.

parts.name: Supracoracoideus intermedius
parts.note: Short and thick. Its origin on the scapulocoracoid is hemmed in by those of the longus and brevis, and it inserts in common with the longus.

parts.name: Supracoracoideus brevis
parts.note: Thin. Origin on the lower portion of the LATERAL surface of the acromion, and frequently the adjacent coracoid.

occurrences.divisionNote: Meers separates three heads sharing one nerve and one insertion region. He warns the longus is the hardest to separate cleanly in dissection because the heads intermingle.
occurrences.attachmentNote: Alligator mississippiensis, from Meers (2003). The three heads have distinct origins and a shared insertion region on the deltopectoral crest: the brevis inserts just distal to the longus and immediately ventral to deltoideus clavicularis. The acromion row is the brevis origin. The Crocodylus porosus row beside this one is Klinkhamer et al.'s undivided segmentation of the same complex, which is a difference in method — CT segmentation against dissection — not a difference between the animals.

occurrences.name: Supracoracoideus
occurrences.action: Wing upstroke. The tendon is redirected over the shoulder by the triosseal canal so that a ventrally placed muscle produces a dorsal pull — the pulley arrangement that permits both flight strokes to be powered from below the body's centre of mass.
occurrences.note: = pectoralis secundus sensu Jollie (1962). In penguins the supracoracoideus is very well developed relative to the pectoralis, which Schreiweis (1982) notes every anatomist working on the group has remarked on. In a flying bird the pectoralis dwarfs it; in a wing-propelled diver, where the upstroke is also a power stroke, the two approach parity. Same two muscles, same triosseal pulley, different force balance.
occurrences.attachmentNote: Gallus domesticus, Abdala & Diogo's avian exemplar. Origin restricted to the sternal keel and the tendon rerouted dorsally through the foramen triosseum, so a ventrally placed muscle produces the upstroke.

occurrences.name: Supracoracoideus
occurrences.origin: Cranial part of the ventral surface of the procoracoid, passing through a gap between its cranial border and the interclavicle onto its dorsal side.
occurrences.insertion: Anteroproximal part of the proximal ventral surface of the humerus only, between the coracobrachialis brevis (posteriorly) and the infraspinatus (anteriorly), without reaching the anterior or dorsal sides of the greater tubercle.
occurrences.attachmentNote: Tachyglossus aculeatus. The attachments here are Gambaryan et al.'s m. supracoracoideus alone, which is the muscle Diogo & Abdala (2010) call the infraspinatus. The two muscles this record's synonym list treats as its mammalian halves are separate bellies in this animal and are not scored into these rows: the supraspinatus runs from the lower third of the INTERNAL surface of the scapula to the proximal apex of the greater tubercle, and the infraspinatus from the external surface of the scapula, cranial to the triceps longus crest, to the greater tubercle just distal to the supraspinatus.
occurrences.divisionNote: See the Zaglossus row on this record for the argument. Howell (1937) failed to find supracoracoid innervation for the big infraspinous muscle and renamed it teres minor, which Gambaryan et al. say destroyed the homologisation of everything around it; Westling (1889), McKay (1894) and Shrivastava (1962) all did find that nerve supply, and this paper restores their identification.

occurrences.name: Supraspinatus and infraspinatus
occurrences.action: Supraspinatus abducts and stabilises; infraspinatus laterally rotates.
occurrences.note: The migration of this muscle from the coracoid to the lateral scapula, and its division by the newly evolved scapular spine, is one of the defining events of the synapsid pectoral transformation.
occurrences.attachmentNote: Galictis cuja. Origin has migrated off the coracoid — which no longer exists as a separate bone — onto the lateral scapula, where the new scapular spine splits it into supraspinatus and infraspinatus.

occurrences.name: Supracoracoideus
occurrences.attachmentNote: Origin restricted to the sternal keel and the tendon rerouted dorsally through the foramen triosseum, so a ventrally placed muscle produces the upstroke.

occurrences.name: Supracoracoideus
occurrences.origin: Cranial part of the ventral surface of the procoracoid, passing through a gap between its cranial border and the interclavicle onto the dorsal side of both bones.
occurrences.insertion: Anteroproximal part of the proximal ventral surface of the humerus, anterior to the coracobrachialis brevis, then along the anterior side of the greater tubercle onto its dorsal side between the infraspinatus (proximal) and the pectoralis (distal).
occurrences.attachmentNote: Zaglossus bruijnii. Of the three genera this one alone carries the insertion over the greater tubercle and onto its dorsal face; in the short-beaked echidna it stops short of it.
occurrences.divisionNote: Three separate muscles, not two — and that is the argument. Romer (1922) derived the therian supraspinatus and infraspinatus from the supracoracoideus of lower tetrapods on the strength of shared innervation, which is the hypothesis this record's synonym list encodes. Gambaryan et al. object that in monotremes all three are present simultaneously, and read the monotreme supracoracoideus as homologous with the reptilian, avian and amphibian muscle outright, with supraspinatus and infraspinatus as mammalian additions to the group. Their membership is marked disputed on that basis rather than the record being restructured on one source.

occurrences.name: Supracoracoideus
occurrences.origin: Almost the entire ventral surface of the procoracoid, passing through a gap between its cranial border and the interclavicle slightly onto its dorsal side.
occurrences.insertion: Mostly fleshy along the dorsal — not the ventral — side of the pectoral crest of the humerus, descending from its proximal apex at the greater tubercle to the insertion of the acromiodeltoideus.
occurrences.attachmentNote: Ornithorhynchus anatinus. The largest procoracoid origin of the three and the only insertion that runs down the pectoral crest rather than sitting on the proximal humeral surface. The supraspinatus is vestigial in this animal, restricted to the internal side of the base of the acromion, which Gambaryan et al. read as secondary reduction following the invasion of the subscapularis onto the inner face of the scapula.

homology.notes: The supracoracoideus → supraspinatus + infraspinatus transformation is argued from shared suprascapular innervation, and the monotreme condition has been its main morphological support. **Gambaryan et al. (2015) attack it from exactly there.** Their objection is that in all three living monotreme genera the supracoracoideus, the supraspinatus and the infraspinatus are present AT THE SAME TIME, as three separate bellies with three separate attachments — the supracoracoideus arising from the procoracoid, a bone therians do not have, and the other two from the scapula. On their reading the monotreme supracoracoideus is homologous with the reptilian, avian and amphibian supracoracoideus outright, and supraspinatus and infraspinatus are mammalian additions to the group rather than its two halves. The intermediate this record was resting on is on their evidence not an intermediate at all. Recorded rather than acted on: the three monotreme occurrences carry supraspinatus and infraspinatus as `membership: disputed` parts, and the record is not split on one source. The avian supracoracoideus is homologous to the reptilian muscle either way; only its tendon path is novel, and nothing here touches that.
homology.openQuestion: Are the therian supraspinatus and infraspinatus subdivisions of the supracoracoideus, as Romer (1922) held and the shared innervation suggests, or mammalian additions alongside a supracoracoideus that persisted independently and was lost only in therians? Deciding it means separate `supraspinatus` and `infraspinatus` records and a re-score of the therian column, which one paper does not warrant.
homology.teaching: Two independent teaching payloads: (1) the synapsid coracoid-to-scapula migration, readable directly off the monotreme condition; (2) the avian triosseal pulley, where homology is preserved but mechanics are inverted. Third payload: compare the penguin. Schreiweis (1982) finds the supracoracoideus nearly matching the pectoralis in wing-propelled divers, against the large disparity in aerial fliers — a force-balance change with no change in homology, attachment or nerve. Fourth, and the sharpest: the monotreme condition is cited in textbooks as the transitional stage of the first payload, and the most detailed modern dissection of it says the transition is not what is being looked at. Worth handing students both claims and the same animal.

muscles.name: Deltoideus scapularis
muscles.developmental: Somitic; dorsal (extensor) muscle mass of the limb bud.
synonyms: dorsal or scapular part of deltoideus (Walker 1973; Wyneken 2001)
spinodeltoideus (Gambaryan et al. 2015, who give the equivalence with deltoideus scapularis sensu Diogo & Abdala 2010 explicitly)

consensus.origin: Lateral surface of the scapula and suprascapula.
consensus.insertion: Deltopectoral crest of the humerus.
consensus.action: Abducts, protracts and laterally rotates the humerus; antagonist of the pectoralis.
consensus.innervation: Axillary nerve — dorsal (extensor) division of the brachial plexus (C5–C6).

occurrences.name: Deltoideus
occurrences.note: The deltoideus is one of the four muscles Molnar et al. reconstruct in tetrapodomorph fish with their highest confidence.
occurrences.attachmentNote: Eusthenopteron foordi. Origin from the thickened posterior margin of the cleithrum just above the glenoid, which Andrews & Westoll (1970a) read as the deltoideus plus part of the latissimus dorsi — Molnar et al. label it 'del?' and note that a comparable posterior flange in Strepsodus and Megalichthys might as easily carry an undifferentiated superficial adductor. Insertion on the dorsal humerus with no landmark: the ectepicondyle, deltoid process and possible incipient latissimus dorsi process are close together and hard to distinguish here, and Molnar et al. hold that for muscle reconstruction it does not matter whether the deltoid and supinator processes are separate, since neither reading indicates separate muscles.

occurrences.name: Deltoideus
occurrences.attachmentNote: Tiktaalik roseae. The ectepicondyle, deltoid process and latissimus dorsi process are clearly separate here, unlike in Eusthenopteron where the three are close together (Vorobyeva 1995; Shubin et al. 2006; Ahlberg 2011). The insertion is still scored on the dorsal humerus without a landmark: Molnar et al. put the deltoideus insertion on the dorsal ridge and its derivatives, and Boisvert (2009) reads the deltoid and supinator processes as a continuous flange in this taxon.

occurrences.name: Deltoideus
occurrences.attachmentNote: Acanthostega gunnari. Origin from a muscle scar on the lateral surface of the cleithrum just dorsal to the anteroventral process, where the cleithrum articulates with the clavicle (Coates 1996). Molnar et al. attribute cleithral and clavicular scars to 'the deltoideus and/or latissimus dorsi' without separating the two, so this row may carry a shared scar and the latissimus dorsi occurrence records no origin at all. Insertion on the deltopectoral crest, where the deltoid and pectoral processes are united.

occurrences.name: Deltoideus
occurrences.attachmentNote: Ossinodus pueri. Longitudinally oriented, anastomosing ridges and grooves along the posterior margins of both the cleithrum and the clavicle, including the ascending process of the clavicle, read by Bishop (2014) as the deltoideus origin — two rows, because they are two bones. Comparable striations on the inner surface and ascending process of the clavicle in Crassigyrinus (Panchen 1985) and on the tip of the clavicular ascending process in Greererpeton (Godfrey 1989) suggest the same origin was general in stem tetrapods. One of the six highest-confidence reconstructions here.

occurrences.name: Deltoideus scapularis
occurrences.note: Corresponds to the dorsalis scapulae of Smith (1926), Howell (1937b), Romer (1944), Walthall & Ashley-Ross (2006).
occurrences.attachmentNote: The fibres pass around the anterior side of the humerus to reach a ventral crest — a dorsal girdle muscle with a ventral insertion, which is what lets it elevate the humerus.
occurrences.origin: Dorsolateral surface of the suprascapular cartilage.
occurrences.insertion: Crista ventralis of the humerus.

occurrences.name: Dorsalis scapulae
occurrences.attachmentNote: Leiopelma hochstetteri. The anuran novelty is a shared tendon: the dorsalis scapulae and the latissimus dorsi CONVERGE and insert together on the lateral face of the deltopectoral crest by a common tendon, which they do not do in salamanders. The dorsal musculature between trunk and forelimb is otherwise largely similar in the two groups. Sigurdsen et al. also fix the nomenclature this record depends on: the anuran and caudate 'dorsalis scapulae' is the amniote deltoideus scapularis, while the anuran 'deltoid' is the caudate procoracohumeralis and the amniote deltoideus clavicularis.

occurrences.name: Deltoideus scapularis
occurrences.attachmentNote: Trachemys scripta — Walker (1973) writes *Pseudemys scripta elegans*, the red-eared slider, which is his type species and the same animal. A triangular muscle arising from the anterior surface of the scapular prong ventral to the teres major origin, from the anterior surface of the acromion, and from the median epiplastron and adjacent entoplastron. **No insertion row**: Walker gives the origin in this passage and does not state where it ends. A turtle shoulder muscle taking a third of its origin from the shell is the kind of thing the consensus row could never have shown.

occurrences.name: Deltoideus scapularis
occurrences.attachmentNote: Scored from Zaaf et al.'s tables for Eublepharis macularius, with the Gekko gecko differences noted where they bear on the attachment. Two heads: one muscular from the anterolateral suprascapula and scapula, a second from the ventral and inner border of the clavicle, both tendinous onto the deltopectoral crest. The suprascapular head is the one that disappears in mammals with the cartilage.

occurrences.name: Deltoideus scapularis
occurrences.attachmentNote: Crocodylus porosus. Fleshy on the disto-lateral scapula, tendinous on the DORSO-LATERAL HUMERAL HEAD. Klinkhamer et al. give no deltopectoral crest for this muscle — the row formerly asserted one, against its own note. The row stops at the bone because skeleton.json resolves no humeral-head site. An elongate muscle attached along the scapula from its origin until it becomes tendinous, lying anterior to teres major.

occurrences.name: Deltoideus scapularis
occurrences.note: Part of the acromialis sensu Ribbing (1938); part of the deltoideus sensu Jollie (1962).

occurrences.name: Deltoideus, pars scapularis (spinous part)
occurrences.attachmentNote: Galictis cuja. Deltoideus pars scapularis, from the fascia over infraspinatus, the proximal scapular spine and the metacromion, by a broad flat tendinous fascia onto the middle of the deltoid crest just lateral to the acromial belly.

occurrences.name: Deltoideus scapularis
occurrences.attachmentNote: Gekko gecko, from the differences column of Zaaf et al.'s tables. Zaaf et al. examined this muscle in both geckos and record no difference, so the Eublepharis rows stand for Gekko too. A blank in a differences column is an observation of sameness, not a gap, and scoring it as a row is what lets the clade rollup say the two species AGREE rather than say nothing.

occurrences.name: Deltoideus scapularis
occurrences.attachmentNote: Eudyptes pachyrhynchus, Schreiweis's type species. Deltoideus major, a very thin triangular muscle arising fleshy from the distal apex of the clavicle, the dorsal surface of the coracoscapular ligament and the acromial process of the scapula, converging on a short tendon that inserts on the caudodorsal humerus very close to the latissimus dorsi insertion. A wing-propelled diver: the flipper is the most derived forelimb in Aves, and these rows are an observation of a penguin, not of birds. That is exactly what species-level scoring is for — the old model refused this source rather than let it stand for the clade. Schreiweis names the **acromial process of the scapula** as the third origin; skeleton.json records the acromion as absent in Aves and the validator rejects it, so it is not asserted here. That is now the third source to describe an acromion in a taxon this dataset denies one — see the element's own note. The acromial process is now carried as a structured landmark: it was described in this note but stripped from the row while skeleton.json scored the acromion absent in Aves. The coracoscapular ligament has no element and stays in prose.

occurrences.name: Spinodeltoideus
occurrences.origin: Edge of the craniodorsal angle of the scapula.
occurrences.insertion: By a tendon from mid-height of the scapula onto the proximal dorsal surface of the humerus, between the clavodeltoideus in front and the acromiodeltoideus behind.
occurrences.note: Zaglossus bruijnii. Gambaryan et al. give the equivalence directly: their m. spinodeltoideus is the m. dorsalis scapulae of the older literature and the m. deltoideus scapularis of Diogo & Abdala (2010), which is this record.

occurrences.name: Spinodeltoideus
occurrences.origin: Edge of the craniodorsal angle of the scapula.
occurrences.insertion: Proximal dorsal surface of the humerus between the clavodeltoideus and the acromiodeltoideus, closer to the pectoral crest than in the long-beaked echidna.
occurrences.note: Tachyglossus aculeatus. = m. dorsalis scapulae = m. deltoideus scapularis sensu Diogo & Abdala (2010).

occurrences.name: Spinodeltoideus
occurrences.origin: Edge of the craniodorsal angle of the scapula, the origin split by the insertion of the spinotrapezius so that the cranial fibres arise over that muscle and the caudal fibres emerge from beneath it.
occurrences.insertion: Terminal tendon on the dorsal side of the pectoral crest of the humerus, between the clavodeltoideus and the acromiodeltoideus.
occurrences.attachmentNote: Ornithorhynchus anatinus. The only genus in which another muscle's insertion divides this one's origin, and the only one whose insertion reaches the pectoral crest rather than the proximal humeral surface.

homology.notes: Present in all six of Abdala & Diogo's columns and in mammals. Together with the deltoideus clavicularis it forms the deltoid complex; the boundary between the two varies with the degree of girdle ossification.

muscles.name: Deltoideus clavicularis / procoracohumeralis
synonyms: ventral or clavicular part of deltoideus (Walker 1973; Wyneken 2001)

consensus.origin: Clavicle, procoracoid, or acromion.
consensus.insertion: Deltopectoral crest of the humerus, anterior to the deltoideus scapularis insertion.
consensus.action: Protracts and abducts the humerus.
consensus.innervation: Axillary nerve — dorsal division.

occurrences.name: Procoracohumeralis
occurrences.note: Reconstructable in tetrapodomorph fish on homology grounds — similar muscles are present in extant lungfish, coelacanths and tetrapods — rather than from the correlate alone.
occurrences.attachmentNote: Eusthenopteron foordi. A hollow just dorsal to the glenoid on the scapulocoracoid, read as the procoracohumeralis origin — Andrews & Westoll's (1970a) 'scapulohumeralis'. The nomenclature is the substance here. Molnar et al.'s procoracohumeralis has two homologues in Iguana, the scapulohumeralis anterior from the lateral scapula and the deltoideus clavicularis from the medial clavicle, so the fossil rows on this record are the undivided ancestral muscle, and the correlate's position above the glenoid corresponds to the scapular of those two rather than the clavicular. Molnar & Diogo (2021) reach the same place from the other end: reconstructions of the deltoid group across seven fossil taxa are nearly identical, and the scapulohumeralis-versus-procoracohumeralis dispute is nomenclatural rather than anatomical.

occurrences.name: Procoracohumeralis
occurrences.attachmentNote: Acanthostega gunnari. Origin from the lateral fossa on the scapulocoracoid dorsal to the glenoid, observed by Molnar et al. on MGUH 1258 and 1300; the posterior fossa beside it carries the subcoracoscapularis. Their general reading of the stem-tetrapod girdle is that the two fossae, separated by the anterior glenoid buttress, mark two deep dorsal muscles with different lines of action. Insertion in the scapulohumeral depression of the dorsal humerus, proximal and anterior to the latissimus dorsi attachment — Coates's 'scapulohumeralis-like muscle'.

occurrences.name: Procoracohumeralis
occurrences.attachmentNote: Ossinodus pueri. Scarring over a large, shallow concavity on the lateral face of the scapulocoracoid, read by Bishop (2014) as the procoracohumeralis origin ('scapulohumeralis'), and one of the six highest-confidence reconstructions here. The same lateral fossa is identified in Hynerpeton, in captorhinids and in Pederpes, and Molnar et al. homologise it with the facet that carries the adductor profundus origin just dorsal to the glenoid in Neoceratodus and Latimeria — the fin muscle mass this one comes out of.

occurrences.name: Procoracohumeralis
occurrences.note: The amphibian name reflects the procoracoid origin; the muscle is the same field as the amniote deltoideus clavicularis.
occurrences.attachmentNote: Called procoracohumeralis in amphibians purely because the origin sits on the procoracoid.
occurrences.origin: Procoracoid cartilage.
occurrences.insertion: Anterior surface of the proximal humerus.

occurrences.name: Deltoid (procoracohumeralis)
occurrences.divisionNote: Leiopelma hochstetteri. Gaupp (1904) divided the anuran deltoid into three parts with separate origins and insertions; in Leiopelma, as in Ascaphus, it is a more unified mass with two or three heads of origin and two regions of insertion. Scored `heads` rather than `divided` for that reason, with Gaupp's names kept because Sigurdsen et al. judge his description still largely accurate even where the fibres do not follow it. The salamander's equivalent is one simple muscle from the procoracoid cartilage — this is the same muscle become complex and often massive.
occurrences.attachmentNote: Leiopelma hochstetteri. Pars episternalis from the anterior epicoracoid onto the DISTAL end of the deltopectoral crest, closely associated with the underlying coracoradialis. Pars scapularis, the most robust part, from the anterior edges of the scapula and clavicle, its dorsalmost fibres from the anterior process of the scapula — a short anteriorly pointed process between the dorsal and ventral expansions, most pronounced in ranids but present here. It inserts on the deltopectoral crest, with fibres continuing more distally onto the shaft, which is the second insertion row. In Rana and Lithobates part of the deltoid also arises from the INTERIOR surface of the scapula, on a vertical ridge behind the scapular cleft that Gaupp described; that ridge is lacking or indistinct in primitive taxa, so it is not scored here.

occurrences.name: Deltoideus clavicularis
occurrences.attachmentNote: Crocodylians have no clavicle, so despite the name the origin sits on the scapula — which is why Fürbringer (1876) called this muscle the scapularis inferior.

occurrences.name: Deltoideus clavicularis
occurrences.action: Protracts and abducts the humerus.
occurrences.attachmentNote: Alligator mississippiensis, from Meers (2003). Superficial and parallel-fibred, lying immediately ventral to the trapezius insertion and overlying the ventral part of deltoideus scapularis and teres major. Fleshy origin from the acromion process and along the cranial margin of the scapula. The Caiman row beside this one gives the origin as lateral scapula from Abdala & Diogo's survey; Meers resolves it to the acromion, which is the finer reading of the same attachment rather than a disagreement.

occurrences.name: Deltoideus clavicularis
occurrences.attachmentNote: Nothoprocta pentlandii, from Widrig et al.'s contrast-enhanced CT atlas. M. deltoideus pars minor: fleshy origin on the lateral aspect of the acrocoracoid process of the coracoid and on the acromial process of the furcula, ventral and lateral to the origin of M. deltoideus pars propatagialis. Short-bellied, inserting on the proximodorsal margin of the humeral head. **The furcular head is the point of interest** — this record is the clavicular deltoid, and the avian furcula is the fused clavicles, so the homology is carried by a bone that no longer exists as a pair. Scored on the furcula without a landmark: the 'acromial process of the furcula' is not the scapular acromion, which skeleton.json correctly records as absent in birds — the validator rejected the row on both counts. Two different structures sharing a word.

occurrences.name: Deltoideus, pars acromialis and pars scapularis
occurrences.action: Abducts and flexes the humerus.
occurrences.note: Galictis cuja. Ercoli et al. describe two bellies, pars acromialis and pars scapularis — NO pars clavicularis, and the word 'clavicle' does not occur anywhere in their 35 pages. This row previously read 'Acromion and lateral third of the clavicle' onto 'Deltoid tuberosity' with an axillary nerve of C5-C6, which is human textbook anatomy, and it was attributed to Rattus norvegicus because Campbell's rat dissection guide was cited alongside — a guide that states no attachment for any muscle. The clavicle came from this record's own NAME. Romer (1924) derived the mammalian teres minor and deltoideus clavicularis from the procoracohumeralis, against Mivart's (1869) suggestion that the subclavius came from this field; that is a homology argument and belongs to the record, not to an animal.
occurrences.attachmentNote: Galictis cuja. Two bellies, neither clavicular. Pars acromialis arises by fleshy and tendinous fibres from the ACROMION and usually the distalmost base of the metacromion, inserting along the deltoid crest — the deltopectoral crest under another name. Pars scapularis arises from the fascia over the infraspinatus and the proximal region of the SCAPULAR SPINE, plus fleshy and tendinous fibres from the metacromion, and inserts by a broad flat tendinous fascia on the middle of the same crest, just lateral to the acromial belly. The metacromion is not in skeleton.json, so it is carried in prose; adding it would be worthwhile, since it is a carnivoran process that both bellies use. The muscle is renamed at every step for the bone that happens to carry its origin, though the muscle itself is continuous across Tetrapoda — which is exactly how a clavicle got written into this row.

occurrences.name: Clavodeltoideus
occurrences.origin: Caudal border of the clavicle and the lateral ramus of the interclavicle, from the level of the procoracoid to the acromion.
occurrences.insertion: Widely on the anterior part of the proximal dorsal surface of the humerus, including the pectoral crest.
occurrences.attachmentNote: Zaglossus bruijnii. The acromiodeltoideus is a separate muscle here, from the apex of the acromion, inserting by an aponeurosis that embraces the spinodeltoideus from behind and fuses with the clavodeltoideus above and below it.

parts.name: Acromiodeltoideus
parts.note: Gambaryan et al. note that reptiles have only two deltoid muscles, matching the clavodeltoideus and spinodeltoideus, and that the submerged position and wide humeral insertion of the acromiodeltoideus in monotremes suggest it is instead a portion of the reptilian scapulohumeralis anterior — whose deeper portion is the therian teres minor.

occurrences.name: Clavodeltoideus
occurrences.origin: Entire ventral surface of the clavicle except its acromial end, and the entire ventral surface of the lateral ramus of the interclavicle, with a superficial aponeurosis over the medial quarter of its length.
occurrences.insertion: Dorsal side of the pectoral crest of the humerus, the most distal fibres by a short strong tendon.
occurrences.attachmentNote: Tachyglossus aculeatus. The acromiodeltoideus is separate, arising only from the apex of the acromion and inserting on the proximal dorsal humerus behind the clavodeltoideus and spinodeltoideus.

occurrences.name: Clavodeltoideus + acromiodeltoideus
occurrences.origin: Ventral surface of the acromion, the ventral surface of the lateral ramus of the interclavicle, and the clavicle as far medially as the sternomastoideus insertion.
