occurrences.insertion: Descends along the pectoral crest of the humerus and far distal to it.
occurrences.attachmentNote: Ornithorhynchus anatinus. The two deltoids are inseparable here and together embrace the spinodeltoideus from below; the fibres caudal to it can be called acromiodeltoideus and those cranial to it clavodeltoideus, but there is no boundary. Diogo & Abdala (2010) do not list an acromiodeltoideus for this animal at all.
occurrences.divisionNote: `heads` rather than `divided` against both echidnas, which is a real difference and not a reading of the same thing: in Tachyglossidae the two are distinct muscles with separate origins and insertions, and in the platypus they are one continuous sheet whose parts are named by where they sit relative to the spinodeltoideus.

homology.notes: Continuous across Tetrapoda; the name changes with the girdle element that carries the origin (procoracoid in amphibians, clavicle/acromion in amniotes), not with the muscle's identity.
homology.teaching: A clean example of a muscle renamed for its bony origin rather than for any change in the muscle itself — exactly the kind of synonymy the comparative tables exist to dissolve.

muscles.name: Scapulohumeralis anterior
synonyms: teres minor (Gambaryan et al. 2015, for the monotreme muscle Diogo & Abdala 2010 call scapulohumeralis anterior)

consensus.origin: Lateral surface of the scapula, anteroventral to the glenoid.
consensus.insertion: Proximal humerus near the greater tubercle.
consensus.action: Protracts and laterally rotates the humerus; stabilises the glenohumeral joint.
consensus.innervation: Axillary nerve — dorsal division.

occurrences.name: Scapulohumeralis anterior
occurrences.note: = scapulohumeralis cranialis sensu Dilkes (2000) and Maxwell & Larsson (2007).
occurrences.attachmentNote: Nothoprocta pentlandii, from Widrig et al.'s contrast-enhanced CT atlas. M. scapulohumeralis cranialis, a thin cord between scapula and humerus with a fleshy origin and insertion. It arises on the lateral surface of the scapular neck, cranial to the origin of the lateral head of M. subscapularis, and inserts on the proximal humerus at the distal edge of the pneumatic foramen. The scapular neck and the pneumatic foramen have no elements of their own here, so both ends are scored at bone level with the detail in this note.

occurrences.name: Scapulohumeralis cranialis
occurrences.note: Gavia immer, and the interesting thing about this row is that it disagrees with itself BETWEEN TWO SPECIMENS OF ONE SPECIES. McKitrick found the muscle ABSENT in CM 2320 — the specimen every other Gavia immer row in this dataset is scored from — and PRESENT in USNM 504983, where it is a tiny parallel-fibred muscle from a short tendon on the dorsolateral surface of the scapular head, inserting on the medial surface of the humeral head at the crus ventrale fossae between the two heads of origin of the humerotriceps. Sanders (1967) also found it in G. immer. It is present in G. stellata and relatively larger in Pelecanoides garnoti, where the origin extends onto the proximal scapular blade. Scored `uncertain` rather than `yes` or `no` because the disagreement is within the species and neither specimen can stand for it; the alternative — taking CM 2320 as the exemplar because the rest of the rows do — would turn one dissection into an avian absence. No attachments are scored: the animal they were seen in is not the animal the rest of these rows describe.

occurrences.name: Teres minor
occurrences.action: Laterally rotates the humerus.
occurrences.note: Romer (1924) derived teres minor from the procoracohumeralis field rather than from scapulohumeralis anterior; the two hypotheses have not been decisively separated.
occurrences.attachmentNote: Galictis cuja. Teres minor, from the caudal margin of the scapula and sometimes by fascia from infraspinatus, by a thin tendon onto the lateral aspect of the base of the greater tuberosity just distal to the infraspinatus insertion. Absent on both sides of one of the six specimens, which is the kind of intraspecific absence `variable` exists for.

occurrences.name: Teres minor
occurrences.origin: A notch in the cranial border of the scapula between the acromion and the shoulder joint, and partly from the joint capsule.
occurrences.insertion: Fleshy in a fossa on the dorsal side of the LESSER tubercle of the humerus, immediately anterior to the subscapularis insertion.
occurrences.attachmentNote: Zaglossus bruijnii. Gambaryan et al. identify this as the m. scapulohumeralis anterior of Diogo & Abdala (2010), which is this record. The insertion is the point: instead of taking the therian teres minor's short route from scapula to greater tubercle, it passes postaxially beneath the triceps longus to the lesser tubercle beside the subscapularis. Compare the Galictis row on this record, which inserts on the greater tubercle.

occurrences.name: Teres minor
occurrences.origin: A notch in the cranial border of the scapula between the acromion and the shoulder joint, and partly from the joint capsule.
occurrences.insertion: Fleshy in a fossa on the dorsal side of the lesser tubercle of the humerus, immediately anterior to the subscapularis insertion.
occurrences.note: Tachyglossus aculeatus. Gambaryan et al. read this muscle as the posteromedial (postaxial) subdivision of the lizard m. scapulohumeralis anterior and the therian teres minor as the anterolateral subdivision of the same mass — which is a third position on this record's open question, alongside the amniote-wide hypothesis and Romer's (1924) derivation of teres minor from the procoracohumeralis. Shrivastava (1962) took a fourth: that the true homologue of the therian teres minor is fused inseparably into the monotreme infraspinatus.

occurrences.name: Teres minor
occurrences.origin: External side of the scapula just anterior to the triceps longus profundus — a fossa for the fleshy fibres with a ridge along its anterior border for the aponeurosis — and partly from the articular capsule of the shoulder joint.
occurrences.insertion: Fleshy in a fossa on the dorsal side of the lesser tubercle of the humerus, immediately anterior to the subscapularis insertion.
occurrences.attachmentNote: Ornithorhynchus anatinus. The one genus of the three whose origin has moved off the cranial border onto the lateral face of the scapular blade, and it leaves an osteological correlate: a fossa with a bounding ridge.

homology.notes: Patchy distribution (lepidosaurs and birds, absent in turtles, crocodylians and amphibians) makes the amniote-wide homology hypothesis weak. The correspondence with mammalian teres minor is proposed but unresolved — see the competing Romer (1924) derivation from procoracohumeralis. **Monotremes now put four positions on the board rather than two.** Gambaryan et al. (2015) identify this muscle in all three living genera, call it the teres minor, and read it as the posteromedial (postaxial) subdivision of the lizard scapulohumeralis anterior with the therian teres minor as the anterolateral subdivision of the same mass — so the two are sister portions rather than one being the other. They separately suggest the acromiodeltoideus is a third portion of that same reptilian muscle. Shrivastava (1962) held instead that the true homologue of the therian teres minor is fused inseparably into the monotreme infraspinatus. The monotreme rows carry the attachment evidence that bears on this: the muscle inserts on the LESSER tubercle beside the subscapularis, having passed postaxially beneath the triceps longus, where the therian teres minor takes the short route to the greater tubercle — which is what the Galictis row on this record shows.
homology.openQuestion: Is scapulohumeralis anterior a single retained muscle with multiple losses, or independently differentiated in lepidosaurs and birds? And is the therian teres minor the same muscle, a sister subdivision of it, or something derived from the procoracohumeralis instead?

consensus.origin: Lateral surface of the scapula posterodorsal to the glenoid.
consensus.insertion: Proximal humerus.
consensus.action: Retracts and laterally rotates the humerus.
consensus.innervation: Axillary nerve — dorsal division.

occurrences.note: Abdala & Diogo mark this cell '– [but see text]' — absent in Timon lepidus but discussed as possibly present in other lepidosaurs.

occurrences.name: Scapulohumeralis posterior
occurrences.note: = scapulohumeralis caudalis sensu Meers (2003).
occurrences.attachmentNote: Crocodylus porosus. Origin on the proximo-lateral and posterior scapula, insertion on the proximo-lateral humeral head, both fleshy. Klinkhamer et al. equate it with teres minor, which bears on the unresolved scapulohumeralis/teres minor question.

occurrences.name: Scapulohumeralis posterior
occurrences.attachmentNote: Nothoprocta pentlandii, from Widrig et al.'s contrast-enhanced CT atlas. M. scapulohumeralis caudalis, substantially larger than the cranialis. Its fleshy origin runs along the lateral scapula from the caudal margin of the cranialis origin to the caudal end of the bone; its thick insertion tendon passes ventral to the cranialis and spreads widely across the ventral margin of the proximal bicipital crest of the humerus.

occurrences.name: Scapulohumeralis posterior
occurrences.attachmentNote: Eudyptes pachyrhynchus, Schreiweis's type species. Extensive origin from about the posterior two-thirds of the dorsal and lateral scapular surfaces; the fibres pass obliquely forward to a strong tendon inserting on the posterior border of the humerus at about a third of its length. Schreiweis notes it is a very uniform muscle across the Spheniscidae. A wing-propelled diver: the flipper is the most derived forelimb in Aves, and these rows are an observation of a penguin, not of birds. That is exactly what species-level scoring is for — the old model refused this source rather than let it stand for the clade.

homology.notes: An archosaur muscle on the sampling in Abdala & Diogo (2010). Widely used in archosaur fossil muscle reconstruction because it leaves a scar posterodorsal to the glenoid.

consensus.origin: Medial (internal) surface of the scapula and coracoid.
consensus.insertion: Lesser tubercle / medial process of the proximal humerus.
consensus.action: Adducts and medially rotates the humerus; a principal glenohumeral stabiliser.
consensus.innervation: Subscapular nerves (C5–C7).

occurrences.name: Subcoracoscapularis
occurrences.note: Scored uncertain rather than inferred. Molnar et al. report that they 'did not find compelling evidence' that the subcoracoscapularis, the coracobrachialis, the latissimus dorsi, the triceps or the individual forearm muscles existed as SEPARATE muscles in early tetrapodomorph fish, though Andrews & Westoll (1970a) reconstructed all of them. The first individual correlate of this muscle appears one node crownward, at Elpistostegalia; under their alternative phylogeny, later still, at Acanthostega and crownward.
occurrences.attachmentNote: Eusthenopteron foordi. A small mark on the posterior border of the scapulocoracoid, suggested by Andrews & Westoll (1970a) as a possible origin. Molnar et al. note that it is topologically consistent with the fossa or rugose area that carries the subcoracoscapularis in stem tetrapods, sitting beside the glenoid near the junction of the scapular and coracoid regions.

occurrences.name: Subcoracoscapularis
occurrences.note: Tiktaalik roseae. Molnar et al.'s character mapping puts the first individual osteological correlate of the subcoracoscapularis at this node — a triangular region on the scapulocoracoid dorsal and posterior to the glenoid — but what they report on the specimen itself, the MCZ cast of NUFV 112, is fainter: rugosities above the glenoid and a hollow above the coracoid foramen, 'well placed for the origins of deep dorsal musculature' and not assigned to a muscle. Under the Ahlberg et al. (2008) phylogeny the maximum-likelihood reconstruction delays the correlate to Acanthostega and crownward. Hence uncertain, and no attachment row.

occurrences.name: Subcoracoscapularis
occurrences.attachmentNote: Acanthostega gunnari. Origin from the posterior fossa on the scapulocoracoid dorsal to the glenoid (MGUH 1258, 1300); insertion on a process on the posterior edge of the humerus just proximal to the ectepicondyle, scarred on its ventral surface (Coates 1996), which Coates held homologous with 'process 2' of Ichthyostega. Where both a recess and a process are present, as in Crassigyrinus, Panchen (1985) read them as the insertions of separate subcoracoideus and subscapularis muscles — the division this record holds as one homology group.

occurrences.name: Subcoracoscapularis
occurrences.attachmentNote: Ossinodus pueri. Scarring over the entire posterior face of the scapulocoracoid above the glenoid and much of its internal aspect, read by Bishop (2014) as the origin of the subcoracoscapularis ('subscapularis'). The same posterior fossa or triangular region is identified in Tulerpeton, Archeria, captorhinids and Pederpes, and as the 'supraglenoid fossa' of Eryops. Molnar et al. rate the reconstruction fairly confident once the character mapping is combined with the scars.

occurrences.name: Subcoracoscapularis
occurrences.note: Reported in urodeles by Smith (1926), Romer (1944) and Kardong (2002), but Abdala & Diogo flag the identification as needing confirmation.

occurrences.name: Subcoracoscapularis
occurrences.note: = subscapularis sensu Ecker (1889).

occurrences.name: Subscapularis
occurrences.note: Leiopelma hochstetteri. Sigurdsen et al. state that the subscapularis of salamanders, which inserts on the humeral dorsal process, HAS NO CLEAR HOMOLOGUE IN FROGS, and they account for the one report of it in an anuran — Ritland's (1955b) subcoracoscapularis in Ascaphus — as the longus slip of the coracobrachialis under another name. Scored `no` for this species against Abdala & Diogo's `yes` for Rhinella arenarum, which makes Anura compute as `variable`. That is the disagreement, not a resolution of it: two sources, two frogs, and a muscle whose anuran presence turns on whether a coracobrachialis slip is being counted twice.

occurrences.name: Subcoracoscapularis
occurrences.note: = subscapularis + subcoracoideus sensu Holmes (1977) and Dilkes (2000).

occurrences.name: Subscapularis
occurrences.action: Medially rotates the humerus; anterior stabiliser of the shoulder (rotator cuff).
occurrences.note: The coracoid contribution is lost with the coracoid itself; only the scapular head persists in therians.
occurrences.attachmentNote: The coracoid head is gone with the coracoid itself; only the scapular head persists, which is why the mammalian muscle is 'subscapularis' rather than 'subcoraco-scapularis'.

occurrences.name: Subcoracoscapularis
occurrences.attachmentNote: Eudyptes pachyrhynchus, Schreiweis's type species. Both heads of this field. The subscapularis caput mediale arises from the proximal third of the costal scapula, a small area of the scapular process of the clavicle and the medial coracoid; the subcoracoideus from the dorsal spina externa of the sternum and the adjacent corpus sterni, further attaching to the dorsomedial coracoid. The two **fuse near the shoulder joint and insert by a common tendon**, which is why one record carries them. A wing-propelled diver: the flipper is the most derived forelimb in Aves, and these rows are an observation of a penguin, not of birds. That is exactly what species-level scoring is for — the old model refused this source rather than let it stand for the clade.

occurrences.name: Subscapularis + subcoracoideus
occurrences.origin: Subscapularis from the EXTERNAL surface of the scapula caudal to the crest for the triceps longus, from the caudal border, and from a narrow strip of the internal surface along it; subcoracoideus from the dorsal (internal) surfaces of the procoracoid and coracoid, bifurcating along two longitudinal crests on the procoracoid.
occurrences.insertion: Subscapularis, bipennate, on the proximal apex of the lesser tubercle of the humerus; subcoracoideus tendinous, descending from the lesser tubercle along its crest between the coracobrachialis brevis below and the teres major above.
occurrences.attachmentNote: Zaglossus bruijnii. Both heads are present, which is the plesiomorphic amniote condition this record's name describes and which therians lost with the coracoid. The subscapularis origin is the finding: it is on the OUTER face of the scapular blade, the inverse of the therian arrangement, and the inner face is taken instead by the supraspinatus and the serratus ventralis cervicis.

occurrences.name: Subscapularis + subcoracoideus
occurrences.origin: Subscapularis from the external surface of the scapula caudal to the triceps longus crest, the caudal border, and a narrow strip of the internal surface; subcoracoideus from the dorsal surfaces of the procoracoid and coracoid, reaching the caudal angle of the coracoid where it fuses with the coracobrachialis brevis origin.
occurrences.insertion: Subscapularis on the proximal apex of the lesser tubercle of the humerus; subcoracoideus along the crest of the lesser tubercle between the coracobrachialis brevis and the teres major.
occurrences.attachmentNote: Tachyglossus aculeatus. Gambaryan et al. regard this arrangement — subscapularis outside, supraspinatus and serratus ventralis cervicis inside — as the most primitive in mammals and probably in all synapsids, noting the half-external subscapularis that turns up in the giant anteater. The subcoracoideus tendon slides over the apex of the lesser tubercle, which carries hyaline cartilage and a synovial capsule for it.

occurrences.name: Subscapularis + subcoracoideus
occurrences.origin: Subscapularis in two incompletely fused heads — a laterocaudal head, twice the bulk, from the caudal border and caudal external surface of the scapula, and a medial head covering the internal surface between the two portions of the serratus ventralis cervicis; subcoracoideus from the entire dorsal surface of the procoracoid but for a narrow medial strip, its origin completely fused with that of the coracobrachialis brevis at the procoracoid-coracoid boundary.
occurrences.insertion: Subscapularis by two aponeuroses onto the proximal apex of the lesser tubercle, the medial head onto a sesamoid bone there and the laterocaudal head onto the tubercle just distal to it; subcoracoideus by four flat overlying tendons onto the lesser tubercle and its crest.
occurrences.attachmentNote: Ornithorhynchus anatinus. The subscapularis has begun to invade the internal face of the scapula here, which Gambaryan et al. read as the derived state and as the cause of the reduction of the supraspinatus in this animal. A sesamoid sits in the medial head's tendon at the apex of the lesser tubercle, joined to it by a synovial joint; the most proximal of the four subcoracoideus tendons inserts on that sesamoid rather than on bone, so no attachment row is written for it. Howell (1937) could not separate subcoracoideus from coracobrachialis brevis in this animal and called the mass together the m. coracobrachialis profundus, having found only the ventral nerve supply.

homology.notes: Consistent across Tetrapoda. The 'subcoraco-' prefix records the coracoid head present wherever a coracoid persists; its loss in therians is a consequence of girdle reduction, not of muscle loss.

muscles.name: Teres major
muscles.developmental: Somitic; dorsal mass. Frequently differentiates in association with the latissimus dorsi.

consensus.origin: Posterior (caudal) border and inferior angle of the scapula.
consensus.insertion: Proximal humerus, adjacent to or shared with the latissimus dorsi insertion.
consensus.action: Retracts, adducts and medially rotates the humerus.
consensus.innervation: Lower subscapular / thoracodorsal nerve — dorsal division.

occurrences.name: Teres major
occurrences.attachmentNote: Trachemys scripta, from Walker (1973). Origin on the anterior surface of roughly the dorsal half of the scapular prong and the suprascapular cartilage. It and the latissimus dorsi develop from one muscle mass and converge on a **common tendon** onto the dorsal humerus just distal to the head, so the insertion is shared rather than separate. Walker notes the degree of separation between the two is highly variable between turtles — absent in *Dermochelys*, incipient in *Testudo*, large in trionychids and pleurodires — so this is a row about *Trachemys* and emphatically not about Testudines.

occurrences.note: Marked '– [but see text]' by Abdala & Diogo.

occurrences.name: Teres major
occurrences.attachmentNote: Crocodylus porosus. Origin fleshy on the DISTO-LATERAL scapula, forming its postero-lateral surface and lying deep to the latissimus dorsi; a long well-defined tendon to a bony ridge on the proximo-lateral humerus — a scar worth looking for in fossil pseudosuchians. The origin formerly carried the SUBSCAPULAR FOSSA, which is a medial site and is not mentioned by Klinkhamer et al. anywhere; their word is disto-lateral, as this note always said.

occurrences.name: Teres major
occurrences.action: Adducts, extends and medially rotates the humerus.
occurrences.attachmentNote: Galictis cuja. From the aponeurosis covering subscapularis and immediately ventral to the caudal angle of the scapula, by a wide thin tendinous fascia onto the proximal medial humeral diaphysis.

occurrences.name: Teres major
occurrences.origin: External side of the apex of the caudal angle of the scapula, extending slightly onto its internal side below the serratus ventralis insertions.
occurrences.insertion: Dorsal side of the distal part of the crest of the lesser tubercle of the humerus, between the subcoracoideus insertion and the triceps accessorius origin.
occurrences.note: Zaglossus bruijnii.

occurrences.name: Teres major
occurrences.origin: External side of the apex of the caudal angle of the scapula and also its internal side, wedging between the insertions of the serratus ventralis cervicis in front and the serratus ventralis thoracis behind.
occurrences.insertion: Dorsal side of the distal part of the crest of the lesser tubercle of the humerus, between the subcoracoideus insertion and the triceps accessorius origin.
occurrences.attachmentNote: Tachyglossus aculeatus. The insertion is on the crest and not the apex of the lesser tubercle, which is the subscapularis' — the two are scored as separate landmarks because keeping them apart is the observation.

occurrences.name: Teres major
occurrences.origin: Along the external side of the caudal half of the dorsal border of the scapula, up to the apex of the caudal angle where the serratus ventralis thoracis inserts.
occurrences.insertion: Dorsal side of the distal part of the crest of the lesser tubercle of the humerus, between the subcoracoideus insertion and the triceps accessorius origin.
occurrences.note: Ornithorhynchus anatinus. The origin has spread forward along the dorsal border instead of concentrating on the angle, and it does not reach the internal face at all.

homology.notes: Distribution is scattered — present in turtles, crocodylians and mammals, absent in amphibians and birds, uncertain in lepidosaurs. This pattern is more easily read as repeated differentiation from the latissimus dorsi/subcoracoscapularis field than as a single ancestral muscle with three losses.
homology.openQuestion: Is the turtle/crocodylian teres major homologous with the mammalian one, or convergent?

consensus.origin: Thoracolumbar fascia and the neural spines of the posterior thoracic and lumbar vertebrae; in non-mammalian tetrapods, the dorsal fascia over the anterior trunk.
consensus.insertion: Proximal humerus, on or near the crest of the lesser tubercle / deltopectoral region.
consensus.action: Retracts (extends) and adducts the humerus; the principal recovery-stroke muscle in sprawling locomotion.
consensus.innervation: Thoracodorsal nerve (C6–C8) — dorsal (extensor) division of the brachial plexus.

occurrences.name: Latissimus dorsi
occurrences.note: Scored uncertain, which corrects an earlier note here that claimed a dorsal humeral scar as its insertion. Molnar et al. report no compelling evidence that the latissimus dorsi existed as a muscle separate from the deltoideus in early tetrapodomorph fish; what marks the separation is the appearance of the latissimus dorsi process one node crownward.
occurrences.attachmentNote: Eusthenopteron foordi. The only correlate is a shared one: the thickened posterior margin of the cleithrum above the glenoid, which Andrews & Westoll (1970a) read as the deltoideus plus part of the latissimus dorsi. There is no humeral correlate — the latissimus dorsi process is absent in this taxon and in Gogonasus, and first appears at Elpistostegalia.

occurrences.name: Latissimus dorsi
occurrences.attachmentNote: Tiktaalik roseae. The latissimus dorsi attachment is present as a process or a series of diagonal ridges (Vorobyeva 2000; Boisvert 2009; Ahlberg 2011), and its appearance at this node is what Molnar et al. read as the separation of the latissimus dorsi from the deltoideus. It sits at the proximal border of the ectepicondyle, which is why they take the muscle to be a derivative of the same superficial dorsal mass rather than a new arrival. In Strepsodus, Rhizodus and Aztecia the reported processes do not resemble these oblique ridges, and Molnar et al. score the latissimus insertion in those taxa as on the dorsal ridge itself.

occurrences.name: Latissimus dorsi
occurrences.attachmentNote: Acanthostega gunnari. One or more ridges on the proximal dorsal humerus (Coates 1996), as in Tiktaalik and Panderichthys rather than the distinct spike of Baphetes and Pederpes; in Ichthyostega the process is probably confluent with the ectepicondyle. No origin is scored — the cleithral scar that would carry it cannot be separated from the deltoideus origin.

occurrences.name: Latissimus dorsi
occurrences.note: Ossinodus pueri. Among the muscles Molnar et al. reconstruct 'fairly confidently' here by combining their character mapping with Bishop's (2014) scars, but they do not itemise which scar carries it, so no attachment row is scored.

occurrences.name: Latissimus dorsi
occurrences.attachmentNote: The largest dorsal shoulder muscle, but its origin is entirely fascial — no bony attachment, so no correlate. The insertion is on the posterior face of the same crest that receives the pectoralis and supracoracoideus.
occurrences.origin: Dorsal fascia.
occurrences.insertion: Posterior surface of the crista ventralis of the humerus, by a strong tendon.

occurrences.name: Latissimus dorsi
occurrences.attachmentNote: Leiopelma hochstetteri. Inserts on the lateral face of the deltopectoral crest by a tendon shared with the dorsalis scapulae — see that row. Scoring both on the same landmark is the point rather than a duplication: in salamanders they insert separately.

occurrences.name: Latissimus dorsi
occurrences.note: Retained despite the carapace; origin shifts onto the internal surface of the shell.
occurrences.attachmentNote: Origin transferred onto the internal surface of the carapace, which is built from the ribs.

occurrences.name: Latissimus dorsi
occurrences.innervation: Thoracodorsal equivalent from the dorsal divisions of the brachial plexus.
occurrences.note: In Varanus komodoensis the muscle is large and its humeral insertion is confluent with that of the teres complex (Kępa et al. 2023).
occurrences.attachmentNote: Scored from Zaaf et al.'s tables for Eublepharis macularius, with the Gekko gecko differences noted where they bear on the attachment. From an aponeurosis beside the dorsal midline — no bony origin — tendinously onto the proximal dorsal humerus. In Gekko the insertion shifts to the lateral side of the humerus, which is an attachment difference between two geckos and a caution against reading one lizard as Lepidosauria.

occurrences.name: Latissimus dorsi
occurrences.attachmentNote: Alligator and Crocodylus, from Meers's descriptions. From the thoracodorsal fascia, beginning near the spinous process of the first dorsal vertebra and running linearly back to about the sixth dorsal rib; a large flat tendon passes between triceps longus lateralis and scapulohumeralis brevis to insert on the craniodorsal humerus in common with teres major. **The insertion leaves a large scar about a quarter of the shaft length from the humeral head, as a tubercle or a pit, and it is present even in hatchlings** — an osteological correlate reliable enough to use on a fossil.

occurrences.name: Latissimus dorsi
occurrences.note: Schreiweis (1982) resolves the penguin muscle into cranialis, caudalis and metapatagialis parts.
occurrences.attachmentNote: Gallus domesticus, Abdala & Diogo's avian exemplar.

occurrences.name: Latissimus dorsi
occurrences.attachmentNote: Cygnus cygnus. Pars cranialis is the most superficial back muscle, arising aponeurotically over the neural spines of three thoracic vertebrae rather than directly from bone — Matsuoka & Hasegawa say the attachment 'seems not on the bones directly' — and inserting on the MEDIAL margins of the dorsal clavicle and the scapula, occupying more than two-thirds of the margo dorsalis. Pars caudalis arises from the neural spines of the posterior thoracic vertebrae and reaches the dorso-cranial ilium weakly.

occurrences.name: Latissimus dorsi (pars cranialis + pars caudalis)
occurrences.attachmentNote: Gavia immer CM 2320. Two separate bellies, 8 mm apart in this specimen. Pars cranialis arises by a short wide aponeurosis from the dorsal vertebrae and inserts by semitendinous fibres on the dorsolateral surface of the humeral shaft, deep to the scapulotriceps. Pars caudalis arises from the dorsal vertebrae cranially and, by aponeurosis, from the medial, cranial and lateral surfaces of the ala preacetabularis ilii — the three ilium rows are that second head, one per aspect McKitrick names, where a single `lateral` row had been standing for all three — and inserts by a 3 mm tendon on the margo caudalis of the humerus, just cranial to the insertion of pars cranialis. A dense tendinous band, George & Berger's 'humeral anchor', ties the tendon to the scapulotriceps.

occurrences.name: Latissimus spinalis + latissimus costalis
occurrences.origin: Spinalis from the neural spines of thoracic vertebrae 2 to 10 or 11 — fleshy to vertebra 7, aponeurotic behind it — plus the external surface of the ventral part of the caudal angle of the scapula and the proximal third of the teres major's aponeurosis of origin; costalis from ribs 8 to 14.
occurrences.insertion: Spinalis by aponeurosis onto a tubercle on the dorsal side of the posterior border of the entepicondylus; costalis by aponeurosis just distal to that, its posterior fibres bypassing the epicondyle to continue into the tensor fasciae antebrachii across a tendinous interseptum.
occurrences.attachmentNote: Tachyglossus aculeatus. The latissimus costalis and the tensor fasciae antebrachii form a digastric complex across the elbow, and one of the two specimens lacked the interseptum entirely, the two muscles running continuous as they do in the long-beaked echidna. Gambaryan et al. read the continuous state as primitive and the interseptum as intermediate towards the platypus, where the tensor is a separate muscle — which would make the therian tensor fasciae antebrachii the last remnant of the latissimus costalis.

occurrences.name: Latissimus dorsi
occurrences.action: Extends, adducts and medially rotates the humerus.
occurrences.attachmentNote: Galictis cuja.

occurrences.name: Latissimus dorsi
occurrences.innervation: Thoracodorsal equivalent from the dorsal divisions of the brachial plexus.
occurrences.note: In Varanus komodoensis the muscle is large and its humeral insertion is confluent with that of the teres complex (Kępa et al. 2023).
occurrences.attachmentNote: Gekko gecko, from the differences column of Zaaf et al.'s tables. **Insertion shifted to the lateral surface of the humerus**, against the proximal dorsal surface in Eublepharis. Same bone, different face, and the shift diff reads it as a substantive move on the medial/lateral axis.

occurrences.name: Latissimus spinalis + latissimus costalis
occurrences.origin: Spinalis from the neural spines of thoracic vertebrae 1 or 2 to 11 or 12 — fleshy to the fifth or sixth and aponeurotic behind that — plus slips from ribs 7 and 8 and a slip from the external surface of the ventral part of the caudal angle of the scapula; costalis as slips from five to seven ribs beginning at rib 8.
occurrences.insertion: Spinalis by aponeurosis onto a distinct tubercle on the dorsal side of the posterior border of the entepicondylus of the humerus; costalis by a first aponeurosis just distal to it, then continuing as the fascia antebrachii.
occurrences.attachmentNote: Zaglossus bruijnii. The insertion is the finding, and it is at the wrong end of the bone: in therians and in extant reptiles the latissimus ends near the lesser tubercle, and here it ends on the medial epicondyle. Gambaryan et al. read it as secondary and tie it to the barrel-shaped monotreme rib cage — the elbow falls in the same parasagittal plane as the widest point of the ribs, so the muscle runs straight down the flank onto the epicondyle.

parts.name: Latissimus costalis
parts.note: Gambaryan et al. state that a latissimus costalis of this kind — rib-borne, alongside a separate spinal head — is found nowhere outside monotremes.

occurrences.name: Latissimus spinalis + latissimus costalis
occurrences.origin: Spinalis from the neural spines of thoracic vertebrae 3 to 11, fleshy to vertebra 7 and aponeurotic behind it, with no scapular or costal slip; costalis from ribs 8 to 15.
occurrences.insertion: Spinalis mainly fleshy along the postaxial aspect of the humerus, from the distal angle of the pectoral crest to the entepicondylar foramen, leaving a distinct facet; costalis by a flat tendon along the posterior side of the pectoral crest, PROXIMAL to the spinalis rather than distal to it.
occurrences.attachmentNote: Ornithorhynchus anatinus. The order of the two insertions is reversed against both echidnas — costalis proximal and spinalis distal here, the other way round in Tachyglossidae — and the spinalis insertion has climbed back up the humerus from the epicondyle towards the pectoral crest. That proximal shift is what crowds the coracobrachialis longus distally in this animal.

homology.notes: Unbroken across every taxon sampled and one of the few muscles whose insertion is reliably identifiable on fossil humeri. Its dorsal-mass derivation and thoracodorsal innervation are constant.
homology.teaching: Best single muscle for demonstrating that a large axio-appendicular muscle can survive a radical girdle rebuild (turtle shell, bird flight apparatus) without losing identity.

consensus.origin: Scapula near the glenoid (scapular head) plus one or more humeral heads along the shaft.
consensus.insertion: Olecranon process of the ulna.
consensus.action: Extends the elbow; the scapular head also retracts the humerus.
consensus.innervation: Radial nerve (C6–T1) — the defining nerve of the dorsal/extensor mass.

occurrences.name: Triceps
occurrences.note: Eusthenopteron foordi. Scored uncertain, and the earlier note here — 'inferred from the olecranon and from humeral shaft rugosities' — is wrong on this source's own evidence. Tetrapodomorph-fish ulnae lack an ossified olecranon; the olecranon and the posterior ulnar crest appear together at the last common ancestor of Tetrapoda, and their appearance is what Molnar et al. read as the separation of the triceps from the extensor antebrachii et carpi ulnaris. Here the superficial dorsal musculature probably inserted on the proximal ulna without leaving a mark (Andrews & Westoll 1970a). Molnar et al. call it tempting to homologise the dorsal process of the Latimeria ulna with the olecranon, and decline.

occurrences.name: Triceps
occurrences.attachmentNote: Acanthostega gunnari. An ossified olecranon process with a confluent posterior crest, present in every stem tetrapod here whose ulna is preserved — Ichthyostega, where it is bifurcated and extremely well developed, Tulerpeton and Pederpes as well. Crassigyrinus is the exception: its presumed ulna appears to have neither feature. No origin is scored; the triceps leaves no correlate on the girdle in Iguana, and none is traced here.

occurrences.name: Triceps
occurrences.note: Ossinodus pueri. Among the muscles Molnar et al. reconstruct 'fairly confidently' here by combining their character mapping with Bishop's (2014) scars, but they do not itemise which scar carries it, so no attachment row is scored.

occurrences.name: Triceps brachii (anconaeus group)
occurrences.note: Multi-headed in urodeles, with scapular and several humeral heads.
occurrences.attachmentNote: Four separately named heads, two girdle and two humeral, converging on one olecranon insertion. The coracoid and scapular heads unite about midway along the humerus. This is the clearest case in the dataset of a muscle whose head count is a naming decision: Mivart (1869) and Davison (1895) called the whole complex 'triceps', Francis (1934) named all four.
occurrences.origin: Four heads: coracoid (anconaeus coracoideus, by a long tendon); scapula posterior to the glenoid and the joint capsule (anconaeus scapularis medialis); proximal two-thirds of the lateral face of the humerus (anconaeus humeralis lateralis); the whole posterior face of the humerus (anconaeus humeralis medialis).
occurrences.insertion: Olecranon process of the ulna.

occurrences.name: Triceps brachii
occurrences.action: In anurans, a major decelerator during landing rather than a propulsive extensor.

occurrences.name: Anconeus
occurrences.divisionNote: Leiopelma hochstetteri. THREE heads, where salamanders have a fourth point of origin at the coracoid (Francis 1934). A head lost, and one of the few places in this dataset where a division count differs between two amphibian orders by a stated absence rather than by a difference in how authors carve the muscle up.
occurrences.attachmentNote: Leiopelma hochstetteri. Origins on the humerus (caput mediale and laterale) and the scapula (caput scapulare). No insertion row: Sigurdsen et al. say the muscle extends the elbow and is well defined in both anurans and salamanders but do not state where it ends, and the anuran zeugopodium is a fused radio-ulna, so inheriting the consensus olecranon would assert a landmark on a bone this taxon does not have as such.

occurrences.name: Triceps brachii
occurrences.attachmentNote: Insertion scars on the olecranon process.

occurrences.name: Triceps brachii
occurrences.note: Attachments are deliberately not scored for Alligator mississippiensis. Allen et al. measure architecture without attachment sites, and Abdala & Diogo's crocodylian is Caiman latirostris. The rows this occurrence used to carry were Klinkhamer et al.'s Crocodylus porosus description and have moved. Worth acquiring a source for: the triceps longus medialis of Alligator is reported with TWO tendons of origin, one scapular and one CORACOID, and that second head is the character Klinkhamer et al.'s Crocodylus finding is measured against — see the Crocodylus porosus occurrence.

occurrences.name: Triceps brachii
occurrences.attachmentNote: Crocodylus porosus, and this row carries the ONLY forelimb difference Klinkhamer et al. found between it and other crocodilians. Triceps longus medialis arises by a single tendon from the postero-lateral and proximal scapula; in Alligator mississippiensis and other crocodilian taxa the same muscle is reported with two tendons of origin, one scapular and one from the CORACOID, and only the scapular tendon was found here. So the absent coracoid head is the point of the row, and no coracoid origin is scored. Triceps longus lateralis also arises by tendon from the proximo-lateral scapula, superficial to teres major and scapulohumeralis caudalis but deep to deltoideus scapularis. Triceps brevis is three-part: TB1 fleshy on the proximo-lateral humerus over the teres major insertion, TB2 on the postero-dorsal and proximal humerus, TB3 on the posterior humeral head. All heads converge by tendon on the olecranon.

occurrences.name: Scapulotriceps + humerotriceps
occurrences.attachmentNote: Gavia immer CM 2320. TWO INSERTION ROWS, because McKitrick gives the two heads two different sites. Scapulotriceps arises semitendinously from the dorsal surface of the head of the scapula and from the ligament between the scapular head and the fossa pneumotricipitalis of the humerus; its tendon runs over the sulcus m. scapulotricipitis to insert on the PROCESSUS COTYLARIS DORSALIS — which is not the olecranon, so that row stops at the bone rather than manufacturing a correlate. Humerotriceps arises from the ventral and dorsal fossae pneumotricipitales, the tuberculum dorsale, and most of the length of the caudal surface of the humerus, and inserts on the OLECRANON, which McKitrick names plainly and which skeleton.json carries as a correlate — so it is scored. Both heads had been collapsed onto one landmark-free row, and the reasoning that justified that for the scapulotriceps was suppressing a site the source states for the humerotriceps. McKitrick records a disagreement worth keeping — there is NO 'furcular' origin of the scapulotriceps in loons, against Sanders (1967). In Gavia stellata the two tendons of insertion are separate but connected by fascia, against Sanders (1967) again.

occurrences.name: Triceps brachii (long, lateral, medial heads)
occurrences.action: Extends the forearm; the long head also extends and adducts the arm.
occurrences.attachmentNote: Galictis cuja. Six well-separated bellies near the origin in this animal — caput longum, laterale, angulare, accessorium, mediale accessorium and mediale, the last itself three-bellied.

occurrences.name: Triceps brachii (five heads)
occurrences.origin: Both long heads by a superficial aponeurosis from a crest running down the middle of the lower part of the external surface of the scapula to the glenoid, the profundus curving further caudal to the glenoid and close to the coracoid; lateralis by a narrow tendon a little proximal to the centre of the proximal dorsal surface of the humerus; medialis and accessorius from the proximal and distal dorsal surfaces of the humerus.
occurrences.insertion: Longus superficialis on the posterior projection of the olecranon apex, over more than half its extent; longus profundus across almost the whole apex from posterior to anterior projection; lateralis on the anterior projection; accessorius along the apical border of the humerus-facing aspect and medialis on the surface between that border and the elbow joint facet.
occurrences.attachmentNote: Zaglossus bruijnii. Five heads, and the two scapular ones are the point: the superficialis arises cranial to the profundus and inserts posterior to it, so the two pull the ulna criss-cross. Gambaryan et al. suggest that suits the ball-and-socket monotreme elbow, which among tetrapods is otherwise an anuran arrangement.
occurrences.divisionNote: A divided triceps longus is listed among the ADVANCED monotreme features, against the primitive ones. Gambaryan et al. note that mustelids carry a second two-jointed scapular head, the caput angulare (Ercoli et al. 2015), which resembles the monotreme triceps longus superficialis; if those are homologous the double-headed scapular triceps is primitive for mammals as a whole. The Galictis row on this record is from the companion paper.

occurrences.name: Triceps brachii (five heads)
occurrences.origin: Both long heads by a superficial aponeurosis from a crest on the lower part of the external surface of the scapula running to the glenoid; lateralis fleshy from the proximal dorsal surface of the humerus just distal to the shoulder joint capsule; medialis and accessorius united at their origin on the dorsal surface of the humerus and separated further distally by a neurovascular bundle.
occurrences.insertion: Longus superficialis on the posterior projection of the olecranon apex, over about a quarter of its extent; longus profundus across almost the whole apex; lateralis on the anterior projection; accessorius and medialis on the humerus-facing aspect, aided by aponeuroses posteriorly and anteriorly respectively.
occurrences.attachmentNote: Tachyglossus aculeatus. The triceps lateralis is separated from the other four heads by a neurovascular bundle in every genus, which is what makes the accessorius readable as a proximal subdivision of the medialis rather than an independent head.

occurrences.name: Triceps brachii (five heads)
occurrences.origin: Both long heads from the scapular crest running to the glenoid; lateralis by a narrow tendon from a distinct tubercle on the proximal dorsal surface of the humerus, between the infraspinatus insertion and the brachialis origin; medialis and accessorius from the dorsal surface of the humerus, their origins completely separate from one another.
occurrences.insertion: Longus superficialis on the posterior projection of the olecranon apex over about a quarter of its extent; longus profundus across almost the whole apex; lateralis fleshy on the anterior projection, nearly fusing behind with the accessorius; accessorius and medialis on the humerus-facing aspect.
occurrences.attachmentNote: Ornithorhynchus anatinus. The lateralis origin has a named bony tubercle here where the echidnas have only a surface, and the medialis and accessorius origins are fully separate where in Tachyglossidae they are united.

homology.notes: Present in every tetrapod examined. The number of heads varies freely (three in mammals, more in urodeles and crocodylians) without disturbing the identity of the complex — a useful reminder that head count is not a homology criterion.
homology.teaching: The canonical dorsal-mass muscle: origin on the girdle and humerus, insertion on the ulna, radial innervation, elbow extension. Every other extensor can be introduced by reference to it.

muscles.name: Brachialis / humeroantebrachialis
synonyms: brachialis inferior (Romer 1944; Walker 1973; Holmes 1977; Dilkes 2000; Wyneken 2001)

consensus.origin: Anterior surface of the humeral shaft, distal to the deltopectoral crest.
consensus.insertion: Proximal ulna (and radius in some taxa).
consensus.action: Flexes the elbow. Because it crosses only the elbow, it is the pure elbow flexor regardless of forearm position.
consensus.innervation: Musculocutaneous nerve (C5–C6) — ventral division.

occurrences.name: Humeroantebrachialis
occurrences.attachmentNote: Acanthostega gunnari. The ventral median ridge of the radius, which usually carries obvious muscle scars and is read as the humeroantebrachialis insertion (Bishop 2014). Two statements in Molnar et al. sit awkwardly together: they list this ridge among the four longitudinal ridges of the radius in this taxon and label it in their Fig. 10F, yet their character mapping puts the ridge's first appearance at the last common ancestor of crown tetrapods, where it marks the separation of this muscle from the flexor antebrachii et carpi radialis. The row follows the description of the bone. No origin is scored — the ventromedial deltopectoral crest scars that carry it in Baphetes, Crassigyrinus and Ossinodus are not reported here.

occurrences.name: Humeroantebrachialis
occurrences.attachmentNote: Ossinodus pueri. Origin from scars on the ventromedial aspect of the deltopectoral crest (Bishop 2014) — the same region Milner & Lindsay (1998) read as the humeroantebrachialis ('brachialis') origin in Baphetes and Smithson (1985) in Crassigyrinus; insertion on the ventral median ridge of the radius. In Necturus and Iguana the origin likewise includes part of the deltopectoral crest, which is the extant end of the same arrangement.

occurrences.name: Humeroantebrachialis
occurrences.note: In urodeles the brachialis field is not separated from the biceps field; the single muscle is called humeroantebrachialis.
occurrences.attachmentNote: Thick and parallel-fibred, crossing only the elbow. It has no girdle head, which is the difference from the amniote biceps brachii and the reason the two are not interchangeable.
occurrences.origin: Anterior surface of the proximal humerus.
occurrences.insertion: Proximal end of the radius.

occurrences.name: Brachialis
occurrences.attachmentNote: Scored from Zaaf et al.'s tables for Eublepharis macularius, with the Gekko gecko differences noted where they bear on the attachment. From the lateral and ventral humeral shaft to the proximal radius and ulna. In Gekko the origin is confined to the lateral shaft.

occurrences.name: Brachialis
occurrences.attachmentNote: Fleshy on the anterior humeral head; inserts on the proximomedial radius with the biceps tendon.

occurrences.name: Brachialis
occurrences.attachmentNote: Gavia immer CM 2320. A rectangular muscle, fleshy at both ends: from the fossa m. brachialis of the humerus to the cranioventral surface of the proximal ulna, in the depressio m. brachialis. Both are named depressions, and both are as close to a clean osteological correlate as this forelimb gets. As in Gavia stellata and Pelecanoides garnoti.

occurrences.name: Brachialis
occurrences.action: Flexes the elbow.
occurrences.innervation: Musculocutaneous nerve, with a variable radial contribution.
occurrences.attachmentNote: Galictis cuja. From a wide area of the lateral surface and craniodistal humeral diaphysis onto the medial ulna and the radius.

occurrences.name: Brachialis
occurrences.attachmentNote: Gekko gecko, from the differences column of Zaaf et al.'s tables. Origin **confined to the lateral humeral shaft**; in Eublepharis it takes the ventral surface as well.

occurrences.name: Brachialis ulnaris + brachialis radialis
occurrences.origin: Radialis wedging proximally onto the proximal dorsal surface of the humerus between the triceps lateralis in front and the triceps accessorius behind, then descending along the anterior dorsoventral line; ulnaris anterior and distal to it, reaching a little onto the distal ventral surface around the preaxial side of the bone.
occurrences.insertion: Ulnaris on the radial edge of the posterior surface of the ulna just distal to the elbow joint; radialis just distal to that on the posterior surface of the radius, descending almost to its midlength.
occurrences.attachmentNote: Zaglossus bruijnii. Romer (1922) held the origin on the distal ventral surface of the humerus to be the primitive tetrapod condition and its spread onto the proximal dorsal surface to be a synapsid advance; this genus keeps a trace of the ventral origin that the other two have lost. Allen (1912) mistook the radial head for the brachioradialis.
occurrences.divisionNote: Gambaryan et al. read the two-headed brachialis as a remnant of a stage with freer rotation of the radius against the ulna, since intra-antebrachial mobility in living monotremes is extremely reduced — a muscle keeping a division its joint no longer uses.

occurrences.name: Brachialis ulnaris + brachialis radialis
occurrences.origin: Both heads side by side on the proximal dorsal surface of the humerus, the ulnaris anterior to the radialis, the radialis approaching the humeral head anterior to the triceps lateralis origin.
occurrences.insertion: Ulnaris on the radial edge of the posterior surface of the ulna just distal to the elbow joint; radialis just distal to it on the posterior surface of the radius, descending almost to its midlength.
occurrences.attachmentNote: Tachyglossus aculeatus. The two heads are furthest apart in this genus and closest together in the platypus, with the long-beaked echidna between them.

occurrences.name: Brachialis ulnaris + brachialis radialis
occurrences.origin: The two heads least separate of the three genera, arising together from the proximal dorsal surface of the humerus and widely separating the triceps lateralis origin in front from the triceps accessorius behind.
occurrences.insertion: As in the echidnas, but the radialis insertion on the radius is shorter; the ulna carries a groove for the flat terminal tendon of the ulnaris.
occurrences.attachmentNote: Ornithorhynchus anatinus. The groove on the ulna is an osteological correlate for a tendon, which is rarer in this dataset than a scar for a fleshy attachment.

homology.notes: The amphibian humeroantebrachialis and the amniote brachialis occupy the same field. Note the naming hazard: 'humeroantebrachialis' is used by Diogo & Abdala (2007) for the lepidosaur BICEPS, not the brachialis. Always check which sense an author intends.
homology.teaching: A terminology trap worth setting deliberately: the same name denotes different muscles in the urodele and lepidosaur literature.

muscles.name: Biceps brachii / coracoradialis
synonyms: short and long heads of biceps brachii (Jouffroy 1971)

consensus.origin: Coracoid or scapula near the glenoid — the muscle spans the shoulder as well as the elbow.
consensus.insertion: Radius (radial tuberosity), and via the bicipital aponeurosis to the antebrachial fascia in mammals.
consensus.action: Flexes the elbow and supinates the forearm; weak shoulder flexion.
consensus.innervation: Musculocutaneous nerve (C5–C6) — ventral division.

occurrences.note: Absent in Ambystoma ordinarium, but a coracoradialis is present in other urodeles.

occurrences.name: Coracoradialis
occurrences.note: The anuran name records the coracoid origin and radial insertion directly.

occurrences.name: Coracoradialis
occurrences.attachmentNote: Xenopus laevis. A long tendon runs from the coracoradialis to the radio-ulna, and in this species it is housed: a partially covered groove runs from the deltopectoral crest along part of the ventral surface of the humeral shaft to accommodate it, immediately lateral to a prominent boss for the pectoralis insertion. Ritland (1955a) reports a similar groove in Alytes. The insertion is scored on the radius, which is the element the dataset has for the fused radio-ulna; the groove is a correlate of the TENDON'S PATH rather than of an attachment, which is why no row is put on the humerus.

occurrences.name: Biceps brachii
occurrences.note: = humeroantebrachialis sensu Diogo & Abdala (2007) and Diogo (2007); = short and long heads of biceps brachii sensu Jouffroy (1971).

occurrences.name: Biceps brachii
occurrences.note: Inferred from the biceps tubercle — an anteroposterior ridge on the lateroventral coracoid, named by Walker (1972) and treated as homologous across early crocodylomorphs by Crush (1980). Level I inference: the coracoid origin is bracketed by both Crocodylia and Aves.

occurrences.name: Biceps brachii
occurrences.attachmentNote: A discrete insertion tubercle on the radius.

occurrences.name: Biceps brachii
occurrences.attachmentNote: A very long tendon of origin from the ventral coracoid — about half the length of the belly — to the proximomedial radius.

occurrences.name: Biceps brachii
occurrences.attachmentNote: Gavia immer CM 2320. A 6 mm tendon from the head of the coracoid, anchored to the ventral surface of the crista pectoralis by a tendinous band, running deep to the insertion of the pectoralis thoracicus. The tendon of insertion passes between the extensor metacarpi radialis and the brachialis to reach the tuberculum bicipitale on the caudal surface of the proximal radius, with a second branch on the tuberculum bicipitale of the ulna. Scored on the radial tuberosity because tuberculum bicipitale radii is the same site under another name. The biceps slip — a distinct avian belly running to the propatagial aponeurosis — is not scored: it ends in fascia.

occurrences.name: Biceps brachii (long and short heads)
occurrences.action: Supinates the forearm and flexes the elbow.
occurrences.attachmentNote: The short head arises from the coracoid process — the fused remnant of the coracoid — rather than from a coracoid bone.

occurrences.name: Biceps longus + biceps brevis
occurrences.origin: Longus just caudal to the supracoracoideus from the ventral side of the procoracoid; brevis just caudal to the longus from the procoracoid and the adjacent lateral border of the stem of the interclavicle.
occurrences.insertion: Longus by a narrow aponeurosis on the radial edge of the ulna just distal to the brachialis ulnaris; brevis further distally by a wider aponeurosis on the radius, distal to and closer to the ulna than the brachialis radialis.
occurrences.attachmentNote: Zaglossus bruijnii. The origin is on the PROCORACOID and the interclavicle, bones no therian has — the therian biceps arises from the supraglenoid tubercle and the coracoid process of the scapula. Allen (1912) denied any ulnar insertion of the biceps in this genus; Gambaryan et al. find one.
occurrences.divisionNote: Two heads, homologous with the therian caput longum and caput breve, but with the size relation reversed: the brevis is the larger in monotremes.

occurrences.name: Biceps longus + biceps brevis
occurrences.origin: Longus just caudal to the supracoracoideus from the ventral side of the procoracoid, penetrating under the lateral border of the stem of the interclavicle; brevis just caudal to it from the procoracoid and the coracoid.
occurrences.insertion: Longus by a narrow aponeurosis on the radial edge of the ulna just distal to the brachialis ulnaris; brevis by a wider aponeurosis on the radius, distal to the brachialis radialis.
occurrences.attachmentNote: Tachyglossus aculeatus. The brevis is the only one of the two to reach the coracoid; both heads take the procoracoid.

occurrences.name: Biceps longus + biceps brevis
occurrences.origin: Longus just caudomedial to the supracoracoideus from the ventral side of the medial border of the procoracoid and a little from the dorsal side of the lateral border of the interclavicle stem; brevis further caudally from the ventral side of the caudal tip of the coracoid, just cranial to the coracobrachialis longus.
occurrences.insertion: The longus fuses with the brevis distal to the level of the pectoral crest and the two insert together on the posterior surface of the radius at its midlength, distal to the brachialis radialis, the longus' share of the common area remaining proximal to the brevis'.
occurrences.attachmentNote: Ornithorhynchus anatinus. The biceps longus has left the ulna: in both echidnas it inserts on the radial edge of the ulna and here it has moved onto the radius, fused with the brevis. A head changing which zeugopod bone it ends on, inside one clade.

homology.notes: The coracoradialis/biceps field is continuous across Tetrapoda, distinguished from the brachialis by crossing the shoulder and inserting on the radius. Both are musculocutaneous-innervated, confirming shared ventral-mass derivation.

muscles.name: Coracobrachialis
synonyms: coracobrachialis superficialis/longus + profundus/brevis (Howell 1936a; Romer 1944; Jollie 1962; Holmes 1977; Dilkes 2000)

consensus.origin: Coracoid.
consensus.insertion: Medial or ventral surface of the humeral shaft.
consensus.action: Adducts and protracts (flexes) the humerus.
consensus.innervation: Musculocutaneous nerve (C5–C7) — ventral division.

occurrences.name: Coracobrachialis
occurrences.note: Scored uncertain. Molnar et al. place the separation of the coracobrachialis from the pectoralis at the last common ancestor of Tetrapoda, marked by a distinct pectoralis process and coracobrachialis fossa on the humerus, and report no compelling evidence that it was a separate muscle in early tetrapodomorph fish.
occurrences.attachmentNote: Eusthenopteron foordi. Two small pits on the ventral scapulocoracoid between the anterior and posterior buttresses read as the origin, and a large, shallow recess on the proximal ventral humerus as the insertion (Andrews & Westoll 1970a). The humeral recess is one of two correlates identified in this taxon and in no other tetrapodomorph fish, which Molnar et al. flag as reason for caution; Gogonasus has a comparable knob-like process on the ventral side between the buttresses.

occurrences.name: Coracobrachialis
occurrences.attachmentNote: Acanthostega gunnari. The rough, concave posterior region of the divided proximal ventral surface of the humerus (Coates 1996); the smooth anterior region beside it carries the supracoracoideus. Scored as humerus/ventral without a landmark — see the supracoracoideus row for why the anterior-posterior division between the two is in the note rather than in a second row.

occurrences.name: Coracobrachialis
occurrences.note: Ossinodus pueri. Among the muscles Molnar et al. reconstruct 'fairly confidently' here by combining their character mapping with Bishop's (2014) scars, but they do not itemise which scar carries it, so no attachment row is scored.

occurrences.name: Coracobrachialis
occurrences.note: Corresponds to the coracobrachialis longus/superficialis of Walthall & Ashley-Ross (2006).
occurrences.attachmentNote: Its fibres run along the axis of the humerus to a distal insertion, so it retracts rather than adducts. Walthall & Ashley-Ross call it coracobrachialis longus; Abdala & Diogo record longus and superficialis as the same muscle.
occurrences.origin: Posterolateral surface of the coracoid.
occurrences.insertion: Medial face of the distal end of the humerus.

occurrences.name: Coracobrachialis longus + brevis
occurrences.divisionNote: Leiopelma hochstetteri. Leiopelma clearly has BOTH coracobrachialis muscles, as described for Rana by Gaupp (1904), against Ritland's (1955b) account of Ascaphus. Sigurdsen et al. resolve the disagreement as nomenclatural rather than anatomical: Ritland's 'subcoracoscapularis' corresponds to the longus slip of the coracobrachialis. That is why this record's division and the subcoracoscapularis row have to be read together.
occurrences.attachmentNote: Leiopelma hochstetteri. From the coracoid to the medial face of the humerus. The coracobrachialis muscles of salamanders resemble those of frogs, so this is one of the conservative parts of the anuran forelimb.

occurrences.name: Coracobrachialis
occurrences.note: = coracobrachialis magnus + coracobrachialis brevis sensu Walker (1973) and Wyneken (2001).

occurrences.name: Coracobrachialis
occurrences.note: = coracobrachialis superficialis/longus + coracobrachialis profundus/brevis of earlier authors.

occurrences.name: Coracobrachialis
occurrences.note: Inferred from a circular depression near the posterior margin of the lateroventral coracoid, shared with Dromicosuchus (NCSM 13733) and Terrestrisuchus. Crush (1980) read it as the attachment of the coracobrachialis anterior. Recorded here as an ORIGIN, which is this dataset's convention for the coracoid end; Crush and Bodenham et al. both word it as an insertion.

occurrences.name: Coracobrachialis
occurrences.note: = coracobrachialis brevis sensu Holmes (1977) and Dilkes (2000).
occurrences.attachmentNote: Klinkhamer et al. divide this into brevis ventralis and brevis dorsalis. The ventralis is scored here — fleshy over the entire lateral coracoid to the deltopectoral crest. They give the dorsalis an anterolateral SCAPULAR origin, which is not a coracoid attachment and is not folded in.

occurrences.name: Coracobrachialis
occurrences.note: = coracobrachialis longus + brevis, or cranialis + caudalis, or anterior + posterior, depending on author.
occurrences.attachmentNote: Gallus domesticus, Abdala & Diogo's avian exemplar.

occurrences.name: Coracobrachialis
occurrences.attachmentNote: Cygnus cygnus. Coracobrachialis caudalis: one of two deep tongue-like muscles from the sternum, arising from the craniolateral corner of the sternal plane and the ventrolateral coracoid base, inserting on a shallow notch on the tuberculum ventrale of the proximal humerus.

occurrences.name: Coracobrachialis
occurrences.action: Flexes and adducts the arm.
occurrences.attachmentNote: Origin transfers to the coracoid process as the coracoid bone is lost.

occurrences.name: Coracobrachialis brevis + longus
occurrences.origin: Brevis from the ventral (external) side of the caudolateral border of the coracoid except its tip; longus from the ventral side of that tip.
occurrences.insertion: Brevis fleshy over the proximal ventral surface of the humerus from the crest of the lesser tubercle almost to the pectoral crest; longus in a sharply outlined triangular area on the ventral side of the postaxial border of the humerus, over its distal third up to the base of the entepicondylus.
occurrences.attachmentNote: Zaglossus bruijnii. The two are separated by a neurovascular bundle in Tachyglossidae, and the longus insertion leaves a defined facet on the bone in every genus.

occurrences.name: Coracobrachialis brevis + longus
occurrences.origin: Brevis from the ventral side of the caudolateral border of the coracoid just cranial to the longus and the subcoracoideus; longus by a tendon from the ventral side of the caudal tip of the coracoid, the tendon splitting into superficial, middle and deep aponeuroses.
occurrences.insertion: Brevis fleshy over the proximal ventral humerus from the crest of the lesser tubercle almost to the pectoral crest; longus in a distinct fossa on the ventral side of the postaxial border, over the distal half of the bone from the end of the pectoral crest to the base of the entepicondylus.
occurrences.attachmentNote: Tachyglossus aculeatus. The longus fossa is a clean osteological correlate — a defined depression, not a roughened area.

occurrences.name: Coracobrachialis brevis + longus
occurrences.origin: Brevis from the ventral side of the caudolateral border of the coracoid except its tip AND from its dorsal (internal) surface up to the coracoid-procoracoid boundary, where it meets the subcoracoideus origin; longus by a narrow tendon from the ventral side of the caudal tip of the coracoid.
occurrences.insertion: Brevis over the whole proximal ventral surface of the humerus, but not adjoined distally by the longus; longus along a narrow line continuing the pectoral crest onto the ventral side of the base of the entepicondylus, at the level of the entepicondylar foramen.
occurrences.attachmentNote: Ornithorhynchus anatinus. The brevis has spread onto the internal face of the coracoid here, and its complete fusion with the subcoracoideus origin at the procoracoid boundary is what Gambaryan et al. take as evidence of the two muscles' close affinity — and what defeated Howell (1937), who lumped them as m. coracobrachialis profundus. The longus is crowded distally by the latissimus, which has shifted its insertion proximally onto the pectoral crest in this animal.

homology.notes: Universal across Tetrapoda. Subdivision into two or three parts is frequent and independent; the number of parts carries no phylogenetic signal on its own. This muscle has the longest synonym list in the pectoral table — six naming schemes for the same field.
homology.teaching: Best illustration of why Abdala & Diogo's tables exist: the same muscle appears under six naming schemes across the literature.

consensus.origin: Proximal humerus.
consensus.insertion: Radius.
consensus.action: Flexes the elbow; in birds, tenses the propatagium — the leading-edge membrane of the wing.
consensus.innervation: Radial nerve — dorsal division.

occurrences.note: Marked '– [but see text]'.

occurrences.name: Humeroradialis
occurrences.attachmentNote: A discrete insertion tubercle on the radius, separate from the biceps one.

occurrences.name: Humeroradialis
occurrences.attachmentNote: Fleshy from the deltopectoral crest, inserting with biceps and brachialis.

occurrences.name: Humeroradialis / tensor propatagialis
occurrences.action: Tenses the propatagium, controlling the leading-edge camber of the wing.
occurrences.note: A striking case of exaptation: an archosaur elbow flexor recruited into the flight apparatus.

homology.notes: An archosaur muscle on this sampling. The bird tensor propatagialis is the same muscle as the crocodylian humeroradialis; the many bird-specific names obscure a straightforward homology.
homology.teaching: The propatagial tensor is a genuinely good exaptation example, and one that students can see in any bird wing.
